# Learn AI Coding

![opencode and ai logos](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/zadrUr1-800x200.png)

**AI slop is here.** It's come for art, it's come for writing, and it's come for coding. That said, four years into "AI is taking your job," the need for human artists, writers, and developers remains. _Why_?

It's the "slop" part. [LLMs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model) are a stochastic reversion to the mean: an **average** of what a human expert might create given the same inputs. But averages are, well, _average_. Good teams want _better_ than average.

LLMs are _incredible productivity boosters_ if you use them with _precision_, _judgment_, and _taste_. **This course will teach you to use agentic AI tooling effectively as a developer.** We'll use [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/), but everything we cover also applies to tools like [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code), [Codex](https://openai.com/codex/), and the rest.

## You Need Coding Skills

"[Vibe coding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibe_coding)" is the "practice" of generating code with AI and shipping it with near-zero oversight. It's what overly enthusiastic ~~product managers~~ [non-developers](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jg1WUOxY6Cg) do.

**This is not a course on vibe coding!** This is a course for people with _at least_ a basic understanding of code, who want to boost their productivity. Non-technical people can _also_ multiply their productivity with AI... but the multiplier is often negative.

## Boot.dev CLI

We'll use the [Boot.dev CLI](https://github.com/bootdotdev/bootdev) to test work on your machine. The CLI has two modes:

- `bootdev run <id>` runs checks _without_ submitting.
- `bootdev run -s <id>` or `bootdev submit <id>` submits your work and marks the lesson complete when it passes.

## [!windows] for Windows Users

> [!warning]
> If you try to complete this course without [WSL 2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install) installed on Windows, you're gonna have a bad time.

## Assignment

1. [ ] [Install](https://github.com/bootdotdev/bootdev?tab=readme-ov-file#installation) the `bootdev` CLI if you haven't already.
2. [ ] Run `bootdev --version` to confirm it works.
3. [ ] Run `bootdev login` and complete the login flow.

**Submit** the CLI tests.

# Chat, Autocomplete, and Agents

![AI Agents VS Autocomplete Explainer](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/agents-autocomplete-sync-1920x1080.mp4)

Not every AI coding tool does the same job. "Agents" became a wild buzzword over the last year, and non-technical people use the term incorrectly _all the time_. I think of AI-use in three buckets:

- **Chat** explains ideas and answers questions. Whether it happens in a browser, in your editor, or on Boot.dev with Boots, it's still just a conversation with an [LLM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model).
- **Autocomplete** suggests the rest of the line or code block when you're writing code. This one is _very_ editor-specific. It's about ergonomics and UX more than anything. Functionally, it's when you start typing a function name and your editor suggests the rest, allowing you to press `tab` to accept.
- **Agents** are where the **biggest boost in productivity has been**. You interact with them conversationally, but on each turn of the conversation they can run commands on your machine, read and write files, run tests, and use tools to gather information. _Agents handle an entire coding workflow._

> [!lane]
>
> Frankly, with how powerful agents have become, my chat-only and autocomplete usage has gone down dramatically. Agents are >90% of my AI coding workflow.

lessons.readme:
# Installing OpenCode

[OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/) is an open-source AI coding agent. It can read your repository, edit files, run commands, and use your local dev tooling to validate its own work.

If that sounds similar to [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code), [Cursor](https://cursor.com/), or [Codex](https://openai.com/codex/), that's because it is. They all do the same thing: let an LLM work _inside_ a real software project instead of just chatting about one.

> [!lane]
>
> I've used Claude Code, Cursor, and Zed's in-editor agents. They're all in the same category, but I think the OpenCode team's _taste_, especially around UX, is the best.

OpenCode is:

- **Terminal-first:** Everyone on the team can use it no matter which editor they prefer.
- **Open-source:** It has a big community contributing to it, and you can see for yourself how it works under the hood.
- **Provider-agnostic:** It isn't tied to one AI provider (like Anthropic or OpenAI), so you can choose your favorite.
- **Optimized for UX:** The team isn't trying to sell models, so all their energy goes into improving the agent itself.

## Sloperator

In this course, we'll be working on "Sloperator," an _interpreter_ for the **SlopLang** programming language. You'll use OpenCode to help you build Sloperator and learn about effective agentic AI usage. Sloperator is written in Python, but _runs_ `.slop` files, which are text files containing SlopLang code.

## Assignment

**Get OpenCode running in Sloperator.**

> [!info]
>
> From this lesson on, the panel that shows run/submit commands for the CLI will instead have **copy-pastable prompts** that you can give to your agent. Each prompt asks it to run the Boot.dev CLI on your behalf.

1. [ ] Install [OpenCode V2](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/#install):
   ```sh
   curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/v2/install | bash
   ```
2. [ ] Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) if you don't already have it:
   ```sh
   curl -fsSL https://docs.astral.sh/uv/install.sh | bash
   ```
3. [ ] Restart your terminal, then confirm both tools work:
   ```sh
   opencode --version
   uv --version
   ```
4. [ ] Install [Python 3.13 using uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/install-python/) if you don't already have it:
   ```sh
   uv python install 3.13
   ```
5. [ ] Clone the [Sloperator starter repo](https://github.com/bootdotdev/learn-ai-coding-starter) and `cd` into it:
   ```sh
   git clone https://github.com/bootdotdev/learn-ai-coding-starter.git
   cd learn-ai-coding-starter
   ```
6. [ ] Use `uv` to install the project's development dependencies ([pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/), [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/), and [ty](https://docs.astral.sh/ty/)):
   ```sh
   uv sync
   ```
7. [ ] Run `opencode` from the project's root to open its chat interface.
8. [ ] Tell OpenCode's pre-selected free model to:
   ```text
   Use uv to run examples/hello.slop using the sloperator.py interpreter. Don't change any files.
   ```
9. [ ] Ensure the agent runs the command and confirm the output is `hello, slop`.

Copy the **Submit** prompt from the test panel, paste it into OpenCode's chat, and send it. Approve the command if asked.

# OpenCode Console

[OpenCode Console](https://opencode.ai/console/) is a suite of hosted services offered by the same team that develops the OpenCode agent. The console gives you access to a large catalog of AI coding models, some of which are **free**, which means you can complete this course _without paying anything_.

You don't _have_ to authenticate to Console to use its free models – but we recommend it, as there are certain features that do require auth.

Of course, **the OpenCode agent can also connect directly to other providers**. In this course, if you don't already have a preferred provider, we recommend using OpenCode Console with a free model. If you already have a ChatGPT, Google Gemini, or other provider account, we recommend _just using that_.

## The Connect Command

Using the [`/connect`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/providers) command inside an OpenCode session connects to a provider like OpenCode Console or ChatGPT:

```text
/connect
```

## The Models Command

The [`/models`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/models) command opens the model selector, so you can search for a model and switch to it.

## DeepSeek V4.1 Flash

If you don't already have a preferred provider – for example, a Claude account with an API key, or a ChatGPT account with a paid subscription – we recommend [DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/console/models#free-models), provided through OpenCode Console.

> [!warning]
>
> The `DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free` endpoint is available for a limited time. OpenCode states that the provider retains no request data and doesn't use it for model training. Still, **don't send private information or credentials** through this.

## Assignment

**Select a model.** _Using OpenCode Console is optional, but you need to use something_.

1. [ ] Run `/models` in an OpenCode session in the project repo.
2. [ ] Search for and select `DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free` and choose the `high` thinking variant. (Or select your model of choice.)

   ![select DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/gYbA4C0-1250x665.png)

3. [ ] Tell OpenCode to run `opencode models` and confirm that you see a list of `<provider>/<model>` entries.

Have OpenCode **submit** the CLI tests from the project root. Again, you can copy-paste the prompt from the test panel.

lessons.title: The Unix Philosophy
lessons.readme:
# The Unix Philosophy

Coding agents work best in projects aligned with the [Unix philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_philosophy): small tools that do one thing well, accept text input, and produce text output.

Fifty years later, text-in, text-out is still the cutting-edge interface for software engineering.

> [!dax]
>
> Sci-fi led us to believe AI would be binary-in, binary-out. After all, `1`s and `0`s are "the native language of computers". Maybe... but they're not the native language of [large language models (LLMs)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model) that are trained on cringe Reddit posts and bad GitHub code. LLMs "think" (kinda) the same way humans do.

**Agent-friendly projects have:**

- Robust test suites
- Strictly enforced styles, formatting, and (ideally) static typing
- Well-organized file structures
- Clear and consistent naming conventions
- Well-written code and a sane architecture

## Vibe-Coding Makes Agent-Hostile Projects

Ironically, the fastest way to make a project "agent-hostile" is to give a non-technical vibe-coder `push` access for a few hours. Slop begets slop. The better the project architecture is, the easier it is for an agent to work well. Once slop gets into the repo, agents will happily _proliferate_ those bad patterns until the codebase becomes nearly unmaintainable.

## Assignment

Have OpenCode **find Sloperator's development commands and fix its formatting**.

1. [ ] Tell OpenCode to inspect the repo and list the commands (but not run any) for:
   - Running a `.slop` program
   - Running tests
   - Formatting the code
   - Linting the code
   - Type-checking the code
2. [ ] Tell OpenCode to use `ruff` to check the formatting and tell you which file needs to be formatted. [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/) is a Python linter and code formatter, one of the dependencies you installed earlier.
3. [ ] Tell it to fix the formatting with `ruff`.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

# OpenCode Config

[`opencode.jsonc`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/config) is OpenCode's main runtime config file. It controls things like:

- Providers and models
- Permissions
- Agents
- MCP servers
- Context management

For example, this config selects the `opencode/deepseek-v4.1-flash-free` model and forces the agent to ask for permission before ever running `git push`:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "model": "opencode/deepseek-v4.1-flash-free",
  "permissions": [
    {
      "action": "shell",
      "resource": "git push *",
      "effect": "ask",
    },
  ],
}
```

> [!tip]
>
> The `$schema` field gives compatible editors validation and autocomplete features.

And if you didn't know, [`JSONC`](https://jsonc.org/) is "**JSON** with **C**omments" (and trailing commas). Alternatively, you can use `opencode.json` if ~~convenience~~ change is scary.

## Global vs. Project Config

OpenCode merges configuration from _multiple_ locations. Your _personal, global_ config is stored in your home directory:

```text
~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc
```

Then you can optionally also have a project-level `opencode.jsonc` in a repo's root for shared project-specific settings. Project values override matching global values, while unrelated settings from both files remain active.

## Should You Gitignore the Config?

> [!dax]
>
> Project-level configuration is _designed_ to be checked in. We made it so that you can avoid putting credentials in there. It's for things that you want to apply for your whole _team_. Any _personal_ settings should go in your **global** config.

## Substitution

Use `{env:VARIABLE}` or `{file:path}` to substitute credentials without committing them. For example:

```jsonc
{
  "providers": {
    "anthropic": {
      "settings": {
        "apiKey": "{env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}",
      },
    },
    "openai": {
      "settings": {
        "apiKey": "{file:~/.secrets/openai-key}",
      },
    },
  },
}
```

## Assignment

Configure OpenCode so it can **run and submit your `bootdev` CLI checks without asking for permission**.

1. [ ] Tell OpenCode to create `opencode.jsonc` in the Sloperator project root. Have it add this new rule to the end of the `permissions` array, preserving existing settings and leaving all other permissions unchanged:
   ```md
   - "action": "shell"
   - "resource": "bootdev run *"
   - "effect": "allow"
   ```
2. [ ] Tell OpenCode to show you the diff. Review it to make sure it matches your expectations.

> [!tip]
>
> Config changes _should_ apply without restarting OpenCode. OpenCode watches its config files and hot reloads them after a file save. This includes agents, commands, skills, MCP servers, and plugins. However, if you need to be sure, use [`/reload`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/commands#reload) to reload the configuration without restarting OpenCode.

**Submit** the tests with OpenCode. Confirm that it runs the CLI directly.

# CLI Config

The `opencode.jsonc` file configures the OpenCode agent, but CLI- and TUI-specific preferences are stored in `cli.json`:

```text
~/.config/opencode/cli.json
```

It controls things like:

- Theme choices
- Keybindings
- Diff display
- Scroll behavior

A basic `cli.json` might look like this:

```json
{
  "theme": {
    "name": "tokyonight",
    "mode": "system"
  },
  "scroll": {
    "speed": 2,
    "acceleration": true
  },
  "diffs": {
    "view": "auto",
    "wrap": "word"
  }
}
```

You often won't interact with this file directly, but OpenCode automatically modifies it when you use commands like [`/settings`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/config).

> [!info]
>
> Don't worry about committing this file. `cli.json` lives in your global config directory, outside any specific project.

# OpenCode Run

The `opencode` command opens the full-screen TUI, which is how _I_ use OpenCode `90%` of the time. However, sometimes you don't want to chat, you just need a single response. For example, scripts and one-off prompts don't need the interactive UI.

[`opencode run`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli#automation) sends a prompt to the agent and returns its response directly:

```sh
opencode run "Explain how our auth middleware works"
```

In this mode, the agent can still read files, run tools, and use the project's configuration, but it won't open the TUI.

> [!warning]
>
> Any permission requests that need an interactive approval will be rejected in this mode.

## Standard Output

Assistant messages go to [`stdout`](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_streams#Standard_output_(stdout)>), while progress and tool activity go to [`stderr`](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_streams#Standard_error_(stderr)>), making shell redirection useful:

```sh
opencode run "Summarize this project" > project-summary.md
```

You can also use `--format json` if another program needs structured events instead of plain text.

> [!lane]
>
> Sometimes I like to have one model do an "adversarial review" of another model's work _before_ I look at it. I just instruct my agent to use `opencode run --model <model>` to run a different model when it's done for a second opinion.

## Assignment

**Use `opencode run` to add a SlopLang example** that prints the result of `1 + 2 * 3`.

1. [ ] In a terminal in the project root, run this with your model's ID from `opencode models`:
   ```sh
   opencode run --model "<provider/model>" "Read docs/spec.md and examples/hello.slop. Create a new examples/arithmetic.slop file that prints the result of 1 + 2 * 3. Change only that example. Run it, confirm it prints 7, and run uv run pytest tests/test_examples.py -q."
   ```
2. [ ] Review `examples/arithmetic.slop` and the command output. Confirm the example calculates `1 + 2 * 3`, prints `7`, and the example tests pass.
3. [ ] If it needs a correction, send another prompt:
   ```sh
   opencode run --continue "Describe the correction here"
   ```

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

> [!tip]
>
> In SlopLang, the `hallucinate` function is the same as Python's `print` function, and the ✨ emoji is the statement terminator (like a semi-colon in C).

lessons.title: GUI Clients
lessons.readme:
# GUI Clients

OpenCode isn't _just_ a TUI. The agent itself is a server running in the background on your machine, and the TUI is just a client that connects to it. And OpenCode ships _three types of clients_:

- The TUI, which is the `opencode` command you already know.
- The Web UI, which runs in your browser.
- The Desktop App, which is a native app for macOS, Windows, and Linux.

## The Web UI

To use OpenCode in the browser, just generate a pairing link with the `pair` command:

```sh
opencode pair
```

This starts the [shared background service](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/troubleshooting#check-the-background-service) if it wasn't already running, and gives you a link to open:

![pairing credentials](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/aqAvl8W-1280x391.png)

> [!info]
>
> You can stop the background server with `opencode service stop`, but I recommend just leaving it on even when you're not actively using OpenCode – it's lightweight and means your next session will start instantly.

## The Desktop App

[OpenCode Desktop](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/#desktop) is a native app for Linux, macOS, and Windows. We won't be using it in this course, but it's good to know it exists.

It renders the _same_ interface as the web UI, and it connects to the _same_ background service. It allows for the things a browser tab isn't allowed to do:

- Native file and folder pickers
- Pasting screenshots straight from the clipboard
- Dragging in a file so the agent gets its real path
- "Reveal in Finder" (or the equivalent on Windows or Linux) and one-click open in VS Code, Cursor, Zed, or Ghostty
- Auto-updates, instead of re-running the install script

## Picking a Client

| Client                       | Good at                                                              | Tradeoff                                          |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| **TUI** (`opencode`)         | Scripting, [automation](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli), SSH, speed | Weakest for large diffs or anything overly visual |
| **Web UI** (`opencode pair`) | Reachable from your phone, comfortable review UI                     | The browser can't touch your filesystem natively  |
| **Desktop**                  | Native file handling and editor handoff, auto-updates                | Doesn't run on a phone or in a terminal           |

> [!lane]
>
> I use all 3: TUI for code-heavy work. Web for mobile. Desktop (very occasionally) for tasks that require native file handling or lots of images.

## Assignment

**Use the Web UI to add a SlopLang example** that prints the result of `(1 + 2) * 3` (notice we added some parentheses!).

1. [ ] Run `opencode pair` and follow the displayed link.
2. [ ] Under "Projects," open the Sloperator repo. If it isn't listed, click the folder icon and select your project directory.

   ![opencode web ui](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/UekeojO-1280x387.png)

3. [ ] Check the model selector before sending your first prompt. Select `DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free` (or your preferred model from earlier). The Web UI may start with a different model selected than the TUI.
4. [ ] Tell the agent to create a new `examples/grouping.slop` file that prints the result of `(1 + 2) * 3`.
5. [ ] Review the file, then have the agent run it, along with `uv run pytest tests/test_examples.py -q`. Confirm that the program prints `9` and the tests pass.

_In the web UI_, tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

lessons.title: Mobile Usage
lessons.readme:
# Mobile Usage

One of the best parts of AI coding is that it makes remote coding _way_ more accessible, even on your phone.

> [!lane]
>
> Before agents, if I wasn't at my _personal_ computer, I just didn't code – it was too painful. Now, if my agent finishes a task while I'm AFK, I check the output on my phone and send the next prompt _immediately_. I'm not as productive as I am at my computer, but it's nice to _be able_ to keep up momentum.

> [!theo]
>
> Some of us find this vaguely dystopian, but we may as well embrace the future.

The architecture for mobile use is simple:

1. Your agent runs on your local computer
2. The GUI (chat interface) runs on your phone
3. They connect through an (optionally self-hosted) [OpenTunnel](https://opentunnel.xyz/) connection

Connections through OpenTunnel are end-to-end encrypted. If you _really_ want control of the connection, you can even self-host OpenTunnel on your own server, though that takes more setup, of course.

## Assignment

_Let's get you coding from your toilet._

1. [ ] Create an OpenTunnel connection in a new terminal (this can take a minute or two to create):

   ```sh
   opencode pair --remote
   ```

2. [ ] Try scanning the [QR code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QR_code) with your phone. You may need to enable scanning in your phone settings. It should contain a link that looks like this: `https://...opentunnel.xyz/auth/connect/...`

   ![opencode mobile login](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/fguhaiY-423x720.png)

_If you get a message like "The app was not found on your device", you will have to manually copy the URL._

3. [ ] Scan the QR code again to log in if needed.
4. [ ] Start a new session on your computer, ask "What's the meaning of life?"
5. [ ] On your phone, open that same session, and ask a follow-up, "When did it change from 42 to 6-7?"

Notice that your terminal mirrors your phone's session, and vice versa! When you're done, turn off remote pairing:

```text
opencode service set remote false
```

lessons.readme:
# Remote Server

You can _also_ use a remote computer to run your OpenCode sessions. It doesn't _need_ to be your local machine, it can be a cloud VM, a Raspberry Pi, or any other computer you have access to!

To set up OpenCode on another server, [ssh into it](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secure_Shell) and run the following command to start the OpenCode server:

```text
OPENCODE_PASSWORD="<password>" opencode serve --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 4096
```

OpenCode prints its listening address, and you can stop the server anytime with [[Ctrl]]+[[C]].

## Connect to the Remote Server

Then, to connect to the remote server from your local machine, run:

```text
OPENCODE_PASSWORD="<password>" opencode --server http://<hostname>:4096
```

_Replacing the `<password>` and the `<hostname>` with your own, of course._

Then, file access and shell commands run on the host machine with the server user's permissions. Be sure to use an encrypted connection like Tailscale or an SSH tunnel; a password alone still does _not_ encrypt regular HTTP traffic.

>
> You may have heard of [OpenClaw](https://openclaw.ai/), a harness that integrates with messaging apps like Slack and Discord, and which can _use_ OpenCode under the hood via the [Agent Client Protocol (ACP)](https://agentclientprotocol.com/get-started/introduction). While it's out of scope for this course, I just want to point out how we're using it internally. Here at Boot.dev, we have a read-only OpenClaw agent running 24/7 on a private cloud VM.
>
> This allows me to `@BootsAgent` in Discord and ask, "How many users signed up yesterday?" or "What's the failure rate for lesson 5.4 of the Python course?" and get a quick answer in a shared team channel!

lessons.readme:
# Providers and Models

OpenCode is an _agent_. The "brain" behind it (scare-quotes intended) comes from the **provider** and the **model** you connect it to. If you don't understand the distinction, discussions about AI-tools can get dumb _fast_.

You'll hear people say stuff like, "Claude is sooo much better than Gemini," and then, when asked which model, they'll say, "I don't know, I just use the Claude app."

Claude Fable 5.1 (slow, expensive, powerful) and GPT-6 Luna (cheap, fast, less powerful) are _very different_ and _have different purposes_. It's _very_ important to know the strengths and weaknesses of the models you're using.

## Provider vs. Model

- A **provider** is the service OpenCode _uses a model through_, like [OpenAI](https://platform.openai.com/), [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/), [Google](https://ai.google.dev/), or [OpenCode Go](https://opencode.ai/go).
- A **model** is the specific LLM you use through that provider, like `gpt-5`, `claude-sonnet-4-5`, `gemini-3.1-pro`, or `deepseek-v4.1-flash-free`.

In [OpenCode's config](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/models), the full model ID uses the format `provider_id/model_id`:

- `opencode/deepseek-v4.1-flash-free`
- `openai/gpt-5`
- `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5`

So when you choose a model in OpenCode, you're really choosing a **provider/model pair**.

> [!info]
>
> The same model can be available through several different providers. The company that trained it isn't necessarily the provider you access it through. For example, `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5` and `opencode/claude-sonnet-4-5` are both valid provider/model pairs.

## Why It Matters

Model determines raw capability. Provider determines the experience _around_ that capability, things like authentication, pricing, rate limits, latency, uptime, and privacy promises.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Tell OpenCode to **set the "model" field in your `opencode.jsonc`** (which sets a "default" model for your project) to the model you plan to use for this course.
2. [ ] Review the diff to confirm the default model was set correctly.

# Model Costs

Although you might be using `DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free` in this course (or another model of your choice), it's _not_ my daily driver for most coding work.

![inference cost](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/inference-cost-1920x1080.mp4)

Every couple of weeks, it feels like a new [SOTA (state-of-the-art)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_the_art) model drops. At the time of writing, some representative top-end models are:

| Developer | Model              | Input Cost (1M Tokens) | Output Cost (1M Tokens) |
| --------- | ------------------ | ---------------------- | ----------------------- |
| OpenAI    | `gpt-6-astra`      | $10.00                 | $50.00                  |
| OpenAI    | `gpt-5.6-sol`      | $4.00                  | $20.00                  |
| Anthropic | `claude-fable-5-1` | $10.00                 | $50.00                  |
| Anthropic | `claude-opus-5-5`  | $4.00                  | $20.00                  |
| Google    | `gemini-4-argon`   | $2.00                  | $10.00                  |

Prices are in USD per 1 million tokens at standard API rates with uncached input and the base context tier, verified October 6, 2026 against [OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing), [Anthropic](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing), and [Google](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing); other providers may charge different rates for the same model.

SOTA models, in addition to being powerful, tend to be _expensive_ and _slow(ish)_.

> [!dax]
>
> Input tokens are generally _much_ less expensive than output tokens, and are cached aggressively, further reducing costs. That said, the _volume_ of input tokens when coding tends to be massive, so they can still dominate the overall bill compared to output tokens.

## Cheaper Models

Move down the price curve a bit and you usually also move up the _speed_ curve. A few cheaper models worth knowing about:

| Developer | Model ID           | Input Cost (1M Tokens) | Output Cost (1M Tokens) |
| --------- | ------------------ | ---------------------- | ----------------------- |
| OpenAI    | `gpt-5.6-luna`     | $0.20                  | $1.20                   |
| Anthropic | `claude-haiku-4-5` | $1.00                  | $5.00                   |
| Google    | `gemini-3.8-flash` | $0.75                  | $3.75                   |
| MiniMax   | `MiniMax-M3`       | $0.30                  | $1.20                   |

[Google's introductory pricing](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing) for `gemini-4-argon` lasts through November 30, 2026, then rises to $4 input and $20 output per million tokens. Gemini 3.8 Flash's introductory pricing lasts through December 31, 2026, then rises to $1.50/$7.50.

[MiniMax's standard pricing](https://platform.minimax.io/docs/pricing/overview#models/text), verified November 2, 2026, applies to inputs up to 512K tokens; above that, input costs $0.60 and output costs $2.40 per million tokens.

Why do input token costs tend to matter more than output token costs, when it comes to agentic coding?

Because you can tell your agent to use "grug speak".
Agents just have to use way more input tokens to gather context.

# Open-Weight Models

Have another look at this "cheaper models" table using the developers' standard API prices:

| Developer | Model ID           | Input Cost (1M Tokens) | Output Cost (1M Tokens) |
| --------- | ------------------ | ---------------------- | ----------------------- |
| OpenAI    | `gpt-5.6-luna`     | $0.20                  | $1.20                   |
| Anthropic | `claude-haiku-4-5` | $1.00                  | $5.00                   |
| Google    | `gemini-3.8-flash` | $0.75                  | $3.75                   |
| MiniMax   | `MiniMax-M3`       | $0.30                  | $1.20                   |

[Google's introductory pricing](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing#gemini-3.8-flash) lasts through December 31, 2026, then rises to $1.50 input and $7.50 output per million tokens.

[MiniMax's standard pricing](https://platform.minimax.io/docs/pricing/overview#models/text) applies to inputs up to 512K tokens; above that, input costs $0.60 and output costs $2.40 per million tokens.

The [`MiniMax-M3`](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3) model is [open-weight](https://opensource.org/ai/open-weights), as is [`qwen3-coder`](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct). That means the numerical parameters, the "weights," are **available to download and run**.

It's _kind of_ like open-source software... but not quite. The training data and training process can still be private. So, while you can run and fine-tune the model, reproducing it from scratch isn't _really_ possible without the code and data used to train it.

## What Are Weights?

This isn't a course on LLM architecture, but at a high level the process looks like this:

1. Gather a massive dataset – Reddit posts, GitHub repos, tweets, Wikipedia articles, etc.
2. Run that text through a training process that adjusts the model's internal parameters, its "weights," to reduce prediction error.
3. The end result is a giant file full of numbers that encode the patterns the model learned during training.

Then, to _use_ the model, you feed it input text and it generates output based on those learned patterns.

When people talk about "AI costs," they usually mean one of two things:

- **Training costs:** the cost of turning the training data into model weights. This is a _massive_ upfront expense for labs like Anthropic and xAI – sometimes [hundreds of millions of dollars](https://epoch.ai/data-insights/grok-4-training-resources) for a frontier model.
- **Inference costs:** the cost of _using_ the trained model to generate predictions. This is what you're paying for when you use [OpenCode Go](https://opencode.ai/go) or any other provider to code with AI.

> [!theo]
>
> For an AI lab to turn a profit, they'd need to charge users enough to cover the costs of running their models (inference) _and_ to recoup development/training costs. So far this has [proven quite difficult](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/06/leaked-financial-docs-show-openai-is-losing-billions-of-dollars-a-year/)!

lessons.readme:
# Self-Hosting Models

You don't _have_ to use a provider like [OpenCode Console](https://opencode.ai/console/). You can be _your own provider_ by self-hosting an LLM. But running an LLM on your machine is a bit harder than self-hosting most "normal" software. The upside is privacy, control, and no per-token billing. The downside is more setup, weaker models (usually), and hardware constraints.

The biggest practical bottleneck is usually [VRAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_random-access_memory), your GPU's _memory_. Model weights have to fit somewhere, and bigger models with large context windows increase memory pressure fast.

You'll hear models described as "X billion parameters." That's a (very) rough indicator of model capacity, but it's not a true quality score. For example, here are two open-weight models:

| Model family | Public parameter info                                                                          |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| MiniMax M3   | ~428B total / 23B active ([source](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3))               |
| Qwen3 Coder  | 480B total / 35B active ([source](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct)) |

At 16 bits per parameter, 1 billion total parameters requires about 2 GB of memory... so MiniMax M3's 428 billion parameters would require about **856 GB just to store the weights**, _before_ any additional inference overhead.

So you can see why most self-hosters run smaller models, often [quantized](https://huggingface.co/docs/optimum/en/concept_guides/quantization) to use less memory.

> [!warning]
>
> Don't treat "VRAM required" as one fixed number. It depends heavily on quantization, context length, batching, and inference engine settings.

## Self-Hosting With OpenCode

In OpenCode, local/self-hosted usage is often done via:

- [LM Studio](https://lmstudio.ai/)
- [Ollama](https://ollama.com/)
- [llama.cpp / llama-server](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp)

The most practical route is usually a dedicated inference server on your local network, likely on a different machine from your dev box. That machine runs the model and exposes an API endpoint through something like [LM Studio](https://lmstudio.ai/). Then you point OpenCode at that endpoint:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "providers": {
    "lmstudio": {
      "settings": {
        "baseURL": "http://<gpu-host>:1234/v1",
      },
    },
  },
}
```

Replacing `<gpu-host>` with your inference server's hostname or IP address.

lessons.readme:
# Payment Strategies

If you're not self-hosting, then you're using someone else's electricity and hardware to run an LLM. If you want serious LLM access for daily coding work, you've gotta pay for it. There are really only two ways to pay:

- **Pay-per-token API access** via provider keys and [`/connect`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/providers)
- **Subscription-based provider access**, for example [ChatGPT Plus/Pro](https://chatgpt.com/pricing/), [Gemini AI Ultra](https://gemini.google/subscriptions/), or [Claude Max](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11049741-what-is-the-max-plan)

## Pay Per Token

With pay-per-token pricing, every request has a direct unit cost. Base-tier, uncached prices from [OpenCode Console](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/console/models#pricing) are, at the time of writing:

| Model                    | Model ID                   | Input (per 1M) | Output (per 1M) |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------- | -------------- | --------------- |
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free | `deepseek-v4.1-flash-free` | Free           | Free            |
| GPT 5.6 Sol              | `gpt-5.6-sol`              | $4.00          | $20.00          |
| Claude Opus 5            | `claude-opus-5`            | $5.00          | $25.00          |
| Claude Fable 5.1         | `claude-fable-5-1`         | $10.00         | $50.00          |

Usage-based pricing may be the most cost-effective option _if you're not using many tokens_ and you're _using cheaper models_. Pay-per-token is also typically the **only** option when you build AI _into_ a live product, such as your favorite baked-salmon-loving bear.

## Subscription Access

Many providers also offer subscriptions for coding, but the tools they support vary by plan. Subscriptions simplify billing and reduce the chance that you accidentally light a ton of money on fire, but there are tradeoffs:

1. Some high-tier subscriptions cost around $100-$500/month, which is a lot if you aren't using _at least_ that much API-equivalent value.
2. Subscriptions are _not_ actually unlimited. They are still throttled and rate-limited. That said, if you're coding regularly, they can save you a _lot_ of money. I get well over $1,000 of usage out of my $200/month subscription, so for me it's a no-brainer.

lessons.title: Cost Effectiveness
lessons.readme:
# Cost Effectiveness

With each new prompt, you can quickly switch [models](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/models) with `/models` and variants with `ctrl+t`. Those are your two main levers for controlling cost.

- **More complex task?** Smarter model, higher reasoning.
- **Less complex task?** Cheaper model, lower reasoning.

> [!dax]
>
> You can waste a lot of time micromanaging this on every prompt. I just use a sane default for most work.

## Monitoring Costs

As you're watching OpenCode do its thing, keep an eye on the right sidebar's "Context" section. You'll see something like this:

```text
Context
147,529 tokens
37% used
$5.56 spent
```

This tells me that my current _session_, OpenCode's term for a conversation, has an estimated _token (API) cost_ of $5.56 so far, which is _not_ necessarily what you pay under a subscription due to the subsidy.

## I/O and Compute Aren't Expensive

Many developers new to AI assume `time = money` in coding sessions. _Not really._ OpenCode can spend a lot of _time_ on a task without creating a huge inference bill. **You pay for tokens, not time.**

For example, these things can take a while without adding much inference cost:

- Running computationally heavy test suites
- Executing SQL queries that take a long time to return
- Making many long-running network calls

answers: Start with a sensible default and adjust when the task calls for it.
Always use the most powerful model at maximum reasoning, especially if you're paying by the token.
Always use the cheapest model at minimum reasoning (users make great QA testers anyways)

lessons.title: Tools
lessons.readme:
# Tools

Tools are how an agent _does_ stuff, rather than just _talking_ about stuff.

Without tools, an LLM can only respond with text in a chat window. Sure, it can _suggest_ that you run a command, describe a refactor, or explain how to debug something, but it can't actually _do_ it for you.

With tools, **it can**.

## What Is a Tool?

A tool is essentially a function the model is allowed to call. For example, OpenCode comes with a `read` tool that lets the model read files.

The agent harness tells the model which tools are available, what each one does, and what arguments each accepts.

Say the model wants to read a file. It can do so by generating a [tool call](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling) – a _structured request_ naming the tool and supplying its arguments, kinda like this:

```json
{
  "tool": "read",
  "args": {
    "path": "internal/api/handlers.go"
  }
}
```

OpenCode parses that request, calls the tool, and adds the contents of the file that it read back into the model's context. The model can then use that information to respond to you or choose another tool call.

It disappears after you read it.
It becomes context the model uses on the next turn.

# Built-in Tools

OpenCode has some built-in tools that you don't need to install yourself. The most important ones for day-to-day coding are:

- `read`, `glob`, and `grep` for gathering context
- `edit`, `write`, and `patch` for changing files
- `shell` for running commands

lessons.readme:
# Specialized Tools

It's tempting to think:

> Bash can do almost anything, so what's with all these specialized tools like `webfetch` and `read`?! Why not just `curl` and `cat`?

In practice, specialized tools are nice because:

- They give the model a **cleaner interface**.
- You can **control their availability and versioning** in the agent.
- They return **more structured output**.
- They let you **control permissions more tightly**.

In other words, the agent's developers can shape a tool specifically for coding work. For example, `webfetch`:

- Can convert HTML responses into Markdown, which is MUCH more token-efficient
- Is permission-aware
- Has built-in timeouts and size guards

As another example, OpenCode's `grep` tool is _not_ just the Unix [`grep` command](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/grep.1.html) or even the modern [`ripgrep`](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep).

It _does_ use `ripgrep` under the hood, but it's also permission-aware, workspace-aware, and returns results in a shape that's better for the model.

## Bash Is the Fallback

All that said, specialized tools are _not_ a replacement for the `shell` tool. Your shell is still the critical escape hatch. It's how your agent can do _seemingly_ anything on your command line, even when no dedicated tool exists.

# Custom Tools

Plugins can [register custom tools](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins#tools) when OpenCode's built-in tools can't handle a specific job.

Once a custom tool is set up, it participates in the same tool system as the built-ins.

## When Should You Make a Tool?

Custom tools are useful for specialized actions the agent performs repeatedly:

- Querying an internal database safely
- Calling a project-specific API
- Wrapping a complicated script behind a simpler interface
- Looking up metadata from a system the repo depends on

The main benefit is a **clean, task-specific interface** instead of forcing the agent to reinvent the same script every time it needs that action.

Every OpenCode custom tool **comes from a plugin**. Defining a new tool for a project/repo just means adding a small plugin file under `.opencode/plugins/`.

lessons.readme:
# Tool Permissions

OpenCode lets you decide whether a tool action should run automatically, ask first, or simply be denied using the [`permissions`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/permissions) array in `opencode.jsonc`:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" },
    { "action": "edit", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" },
    { "action": "webfetch", "resource": "*", "effect": "deny" },
  ],
}
```

Each rule's `effect` is one of:

- `allow`: run without approval
- `ask`: prompt before running
- `deny`: block the action

Each rule matches an `action` and a `resource`. A resource can be a path, command, URL, search query, skill ID, or subagent ID. Both fields support wildcards.

For example, this changes the default behavior for both `webfetch` and `websearch` to `ask`:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [{ "action": "web*", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" }],
}
```

> [!tip]
>
> Rules are evaluated in order, and the **last matching rule wins**, so put broad defaults first and narrow exceptions later.

## Default Behavior

OpenCode starts _fairly_ permissive for most tools:

- Most permissions default to `allow`
- `external_directory` (accessing directories outside where OpenCode was started) defaults to `allow`
- `read` is allowed by default, but `.env` files default to `ask`

One permission [action](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/permissions#actions) can cover several related tools:

- `edit` controls the `edit`, `write`, and `patch` tools.
- `shell` controls shell commands.
- `subagent` controls which child agents may run.

## Assignment

**Configure which tools OpenCode can use without asking.**

1. [ ] Tell OpenCode to update `opencode.jsonc` so `run_slop` and `bootdev run` commands are allowed, while other shell commands require approval. Put these rules at the end, with the broad shell rule _before_ the `bootdev` exception.

lessons.readme:
# Sandboxing

If you've ever thought,

> Gee, maybe it isn't smart to allow a stochastic parrot to access all the data on my machine and execute arbitrary code...

rest assured, you're not crazy. That's where [sandboxing](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandbox_(computer_security)>) comes in. You run OpenCode, or something even more autonomous like [OpenClaw](https://openclaw.ai/), in an **isolated environment** with limited access to your files, credentials, and network.

Then, if it does something dumb, you've at least limited the blast radius. The degree of protection depends on how heavily you locked down the environment.

## When Should You Sandbox?

Sandboxing is especially useful when you're running unfamiliar code or dependency install scripts, working near sensitive data, or letting an agent run more autonomously with fewer approval prompts.

For a familiar project, you may choose to work directly on your dev machine and review any dangerous tool requests. But approving a command does _not_ isolate the code it runs, and careful prompts don't guarantee safe behavior.

## How to Sandbox

There are about as many ways to sandbox as there are to skin a cat.

- You can buy a separate machine and run OpenCode there.
- You can run OpenCode in a dedicated virtual machine locally or in the cloud.
- You can run OpenCode in a [Docker container](https://www.docker.com/) or [Docker Sandbox](https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/) with access only to the project files it needs.

There isn't a right answer, but be deliberate about what you share with the model! A container can still change a host folder that you [mount with write access](https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/bind-mounts/#considerations-and-constraints). Credentials and network access can also let code inside the sandbox affect systems outside it.

> [!tip]
>
> One benefit of sandboxing that may surprise you is _productivity_. In a disposable environment with limited access, you can be **much more permissive** with your agent and let it run for longer without needing to babysit it the whole time.

It doesn't matter, the AI will always escape confinement.

# Prompting

Ever heard the term "[prompt engineering](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering?api-mode=responses#prompt-engineering)"? There were a few months in 2025 when the talking heads were saying things like:

> Don't be a software engineer, be a prompt engineer.

As it turns out, being a good "prompt engineer" is just **being a good software engineer that follows a few best practices** when working with agents.

![AI Prompting Explainer](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/Ai-Prompting-V2-1920x1080.mp4)

## What Doesn't Make a Good Prompt?

Unsurprisingly, [shouting](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JeNS1ZNHQs8):

> YOU ARE A 10X SENIOR ENGINEER AT META. DESIGN MY APP LIKE THE BABY OF JOHN CARMACK AND LINUS TORVALDS WOULD.

is _not_ an effective prompting tactic.

## What Makes a Good Prompt?

- Be specific (you need strong technical skills to be able to do this)
- Define constraints
- Add meaningful context
- Describe edge cases
- Provide validation instructions

Your agent is _exceptionally good_ at:

- Applying code changes quickly
- Spotting patterns and searching for code related to the task
- Ensuring tests, linters, and formatters pass

Your agent _does not_:

- Understand your customers or business goals inherently
- Have full context of the history or future plans for the project
- Have a complete understanding of any architecture that lives outside the repo
- Know how the running system behaves (unless you've provided logs or other context, which is a good idea)
- Care _nearly_ as much as you do about keeping the "lines of code" count sane
- **Have taste**

## Assignment

Sloperator's `\t` escape is broken: it produces the letter `t` instead of a tab character.

1. [ ] See it for yourself. Create a new `examples/tab.slop`:
   ```slop

   hallucinate(“name\tscore”)✨
   ```
2. [ ] Run it:

   ```sh
   uv run sloperator.py examples/tab.slop
   ```

   You'll get `nametscore`, when you should get `name` and `score` with a tab between them!

3. [ ] Write a prompt that gets OpenCode to fix the escape. Use the checklist above:
   1. [ ] Point it at the right code.
   2. [ ] Constrain what it's allowed to change.
   3. [ ] Give it a way to prove the fix worked.
4. [ ] Run `examples/tab.slop` again and confirm you get a real tab.

# Plan Agent

OpenCode ships with two built-in primary [agents](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/agents):

- **Build (default):** The agent can _take action_ on the codebase: edit files, run commands, use tools.
- **Plan:** The agent can inspect the project, run shell commands, ask questions, and plan changes. OpenCode blocks its `edit`, `write`, and `patch` tool calls from modifying project files – except for dedicated plan files.

> [!dax]
>
> I've almost stopped using Plan agents entirely. It's a personal preference, but I just talk to the agent in Build mode, iterate on actual code changes, and eventually arrive at a final solution. The model is smart enough to know we're planning and not actually make changes yet.
>
> If I do want an intermediary step where I create a checklist, I just stay in Build mode and have it write a Markdown file for me.

Okay, so whether you actually switch to "plan" or just plan-in-build mode is up to you, but there are still some best practices to consider:

- **If _you're_ confident** about what you want, force the agent to write a plan, then review it and clarify any points before it implements.
- **If _you're not_ confident** about what you want, force the agent to _ask you_ clarifying questions before it proposes a plan.

> [!lane]
>
> Making your agent ask you questions is one of the best "productivity hacks", particularly when you're feeling blocked on a task. In my experience, agents are much better at helping _you_ brainstorm and clarify _your_ ideas, than they are at producing creative ideas on their own.

## Assignment

**Plan and add support for the `loadbearing` keyword**, SlopLang's immutable variable declaration (like `const` in other languages). For example:

```slop
loadbearing LIMIT = 100✨
slop score = 10✨

— allowed
score = score + 1✨

— not allowed
LIMIT = 200✨
```

`score` can be reassigned, `LIMIT` can't, so that last line should be a runtime error: `cannot assign to loadbearing 'LIMIT'`.

1. [ ] Press [[Shift]]+[[Tab]] to cycle agents until **Plan** is selected. Tell it to investigate adding `loadbearing`, and have it _ask you_ about unresolved behavior before proposing an implementation.
2. [ ] Answer the agent's questions and agree on a plan. A `loadbearing` declaration:

   - Should reject reassignment with the message `cannot assign to loadbearing '<name>'`
   - Cannot be redeclared in the same scope
   - Should be documented in `docs/spec.md`
3. [ ] Use [[Shift]]+[[Tab]] to switch back to **Build** and tell it to implement the plan, add tests, and update `docs/spec.md`.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

lessons.readme:
# Canceling

One of the easiest ways to ~~make [`@sama`](https://x.com/sama) a lot of money~~ waste tokens with coding agents is to let a bad loop continue for too long.

If you're watching your agent work (and let's be frank, most of the time you actually _shouldn't_ be), you'll see the tools it's calling, the changes it's making, and the reasoning it's producing in real time. If something looks off, press [[Esc]] twice to cancel the loop.

Just correct the bad behavior with a new prompt and try again. Canceling preserves the conversation context and doesn't undo changes already made.

> [!lane]
>
> After I fire off a prompt I _usually_ tab away to work on something else (that's one of the main productivity boosts of using an agent). That said, sometimes I hang around for about 10 seconds, especially if it's a particularly large task, just to make sure things got off to a good start.

## Adding a Cancel Condition

Another big-brain strat is to bake a "cancel condition" directly into your prompt. This is super useful if the start of the task is "research" and the next step is "implement". If the research comes back with less than optimal results, you want the agent to stop and ask you what to do next, rather than blindly implement a bad plan. For example:

> If you can't find an API endpoint that matches the functionality we need, pause and ask me what to do next.

# Steering

Now, sometimes you fire off a prompt and immediately realize you forgot to mention something important.

You _could_ press [[Esc]] twice to cancel the run, then send a new prompt. Instead, just **steer** it: type the new prompt and press [[Enter]] while the agent is still running.

A steering message gets picked up at the next _step boundary_ (usually as soon as the tool calls it's running finish). The agent then keeps going on the same task with your new information in context.

A steering message should have a grey left border to indicate the agent hasn't read it yet (unless you've changed OpenCode's theme):

# The Prompt Box

OpenCode's prompt box does more than just accept raw text. It has some nice ergonomic features that are worth knowing about.

## Selecting Files

Type `@` and start typing a filename. OpenCode will open a menu you can navigate with the arrow keys, then you can press [[Enter]] to attach it. For example:

```text
Explain how functions work in @docs/spec.md
```

Selecting a text file has OpenCode _read it into your prompt_. That saves the model from having to request a read-file tool call, though large files can be truncated.

## Shortcuts

Some [default TUI shortcuts](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/keybinds#input-editing) include:

- [[Enter]] sends the prompt. While the agent is working, it sends a steering message.
- [[Shift]]+[[Enter]] adds a newline. If your terminal doesn't support that combination, try [[Ctrl]]+[[Enter]] or [[Ctrl]]+[[J]].
- [[Up]] recalls an earlier prompt when the cursor is at the start of the input. [[Down]] moves forward through prompt history when the cursor is at the end.
- [[Ctrl]]+[[C]] clears the input field or, if the input is already clear, exits OpenCode.
- [[Ctrl]]+[[X]], then [[E]], opens your prompt in your external editor (`VISUAL`, or `EDITOR` if `VISUAL` isn't set). Save and close the editor; OpenCode reads the draft back when the editor process exits. GUI editors need a wait flag, such as `code --wait`.

## Copy/Paste

You can paste text normally into the prompt box. By default, long pastes appear as a compact label. Don't worry, OpenCode still gets the full text.

![paste box](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/Y5pWEEs-454x148.png)

By default, selecting text with the mouse in the TUI copies it to your clipboard. You'll see a "Copied to clipboard" toast when it succeeds.

## Shell Mode

Type `!` at the start of an empty prompt to enter shell mode. It runs a shell command directly, without asking the model to run it. It's useful for quick commands, not interactive terminal programs.

That said, the command and its output become part of the session, so your next prompt can refer to the result. You can use [[Esc]] to leave shell mode without running anything.

## Assignment

**Create a doubling example** using the prompt box. This SlopLang code doubles a number and prints the result:

```slop
clanker double(number) {
    ship number * 2✨
}
hallucinate(double(21))✨ — prints 42
```

1. [ ] In the TUI prompt box, use `@` to select `docs/spec.md` and `examples/hello.slop`.
2. [ ] Write a multiline prompt asking OpenCode to create `examples/doubling.slop` with the behavior above, but to double the number 13 (producing 26). Use [[Shift]]+[[Enter]] or [[Ctrl]]+[[J]] to separate the task from its expected output, then send it.
3. [ ] In an empty prompt box, type `!` and run `uv run sloperator.py examples/doubling.slop` in shell mode. Confirm that it prints `26`.
4. [ ] Back in the normal prompt box, use [[Up]] to find the prompt you sent in step 2 (you may need to press it more than once). Inspect it, then clear it without sending it again.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

# Queueing

Steering blends your message into the task the agent is already working on, but sometimes you don't want that.

Say the agent is fixing a bug and you want the formatter run when it's done. Not a correction, but a **follow-up**. That's what _queueing_ is for.

To queue a prompt, type it in, then press [[Ctrl]]+[[X]] before [[Enter]] to send it. The agent will finish its entire current task, then pick up the queued prompt and start working on that.

- **Steer**: changes the work in flight (default)
- **Queue**: waits until the current work is done, then sends the next prompt ([[Ctrl]]+[[X]] before [[Enter]])

A queued message should be clearly indicated with the word "queued":

![queued message](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/FZnA3Yn-1280x188.png)

## Assignment

**Queue a follow-up** while OpenCode fixes Sloperator's division-by-zero error. This SlopLang code:

```slop
hallucinate(1 / 0)✨
```

It should produce a nice SlopLang runtime error message, not a Python traceback.

lessons.title: Prompt Examples
lessons.readme:
# Prompt Examples

Prompting isn't a dark art. **I'd take a technical domain expert who understands their customer** over someone with a "Prompting for Dummies" cheatsheet any day.

It's easy to learn to write better prompts. It's hard to learn to code and understand your customers' needs. That said, there are some basic rules to be aware of. Some providers even have guides on writing better prompts:

- [OpenAI's Prompt Guidance](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering)
- [Anthropic's Prompt Best Practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)
- [Google's Prompt Design Strategies](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies)

But you're here for _our_ opinions, so here are a few more examples of good and bad prompts.

> [!info]
>
> The following examples are of a software developer using AI to write code for a hypothetical online shopping site, like Amazon.com.

## Clarify Scope

**Worse:**

> Customer reviews aren't displaying large enough to be easily read; increase the font size.

**Better:**

> Customer reviews _on the product checkout page_ are hard to read; increase the font size _of those reviews only_.

Without a clear understanding of _where_ and _how much_ to update, the agent may choose to update a single file, or every related function across the codebase.

## Provide Implementation Constraints

**Worse:**

> Customer reviews on the product checkout page are hard to read; increase the font size of those reviews only.

**Better:**

> Customer reviews on the product checkout page are hard to read; increase the font size of those reviews only. _If the function is shared, allow configurable font size via parameters_.

AI agents will often over-abstract or under-abstract aggressively, either by creating parameters that are never actually used, or on the contrary, reconstructing entirely new implementations that could have just been a new parameter.

> [!dax]
>
> AI can't produce good code without you.

## Point the AI to Existing Patterns

**Worse:**

> The checkout page currently always shows the price in US dollars. It should localize the price to the user's currency.

**Better:**

> The checkout page currently always shows the price in US dollars. It should localize the price to the user's currency. _Take a look at the gift-code page, which already implements this pattern_.

The model **REALLY** wants to solve the problem, and it won't always scan your entire codebase perfectly to find existing patterns, especially if they're not easily found via a keyword-based regex. Tell it where to look if you already know the place.

## Break Massive Tasks Into Smaller Steps

**Worse:**

> Build me a new checkout experience from scratch using Stripe.

**Better:**

> Build a new checkout page component on the frontend, using mock data for now.

_Then work with the agent to get the UI the way you want it..._

> Add the backend endpoints necessary for the checkout page to function, and update the frontend accordingly to use them.

_Then work with the agent to hook up the backend logic..._

This one depends on **how much planning you've done**. If you wrote a detailed architecture prompt or had a long Plan session already, you _can_ try to one-shot bigger tasks. It's higher-risk, higher-reward. If you step away and let the model cook, there's a good chance it goes off the rails early in a way that was _entirely preventable_.

lessons.title: Speech to Text
lessons.readme:
# Speech to Text

Often, you already have the context your agent needs in your head, but typing it out is a **huge pain in the butt**.

Using [speech-to-text](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speech_recognition) (STT) to do brain dumps is probably the highest-impact/lowest-effort improvement you can make to your prompting.

## Agents Summarize Well

You don't need to polish a spoken prompt as you would a PR description meant for a human. Agents have no problem understanding messy wording and corrections like "Um, actually, forget that, do this other thing," but what helps is the _extra context_ you provide, not the additional words themselves.

A typed prompt might look like this:

> Fix the checkout bug where discounts don't apply correctly.

Whereas a spoken prompt will look more like this:

> Fix the checkout bug where discounts don't apply correctly. I think it only happens when the user has both a promo code and store credit. The old checkout flow handled this in `applyCredits`, but the new flow moved discount logic into the payment step. Please compare those paths before changing anything, and don't rewrite the whole checkout pipeline unless you find a real reason. Oh, and I think Dan made a PR about this 5 or 6 days ago; you can probably find that commit on the `main` branch.

That second prompt is messier, but it's _much_ more useful to an agent.

> [!dax]
>
> For agent prompts, **voice should be your default input method**.

## Which Tool to Use?

Some agent harnesses have STT built in, but honestly, we prefer to use a dedicated tool that will work the same way across your entire machine. After all, you might want to use it for tasks _other_ than prompting in OpenCode.

[Handy](https://handy.computer/) is a good default speech-to-text tool that works on Linux, macOS, and Windows. I've configured it so that:

1. I move my cursor into the text input I'm working with (like OpenCode's prompt field).
2. I hold down [[Ctrl]]+[[Alt]]+[[Cmd]] to start recording (it's a psychotic key combo, I know... but hey, it doesn't conflict with anything).
3. I speak my prompt.
4. I release [[Ctrl]]+[[Alt]]+[[Cmd]], and the words are ~instantly pasted into the focused text input (it's wild how fast it is).

[Hex](https://github.com/anomalyco/hex#readme) is another solid option for Apple silicon, with Windows and Linux builds in beta.

> [!theo]
>
> My favorite thing about these speech-to-text tools is that they use local models. The recordings of your voice never leave your machine.

## Assignment

**Use your voice** to give OpenCode a real task.

1. [ ] Set up [Handy](https://handy.computer/) or another dictation tool if you don't already have one.
2. [ ] Dictate a prompt telling OpenCode to create a new `examples/countdown.slop` file. It should contain SlopLang code that prints `3`, `2`, and `1` on separate lines, then prints `liftoff`. Review the transcription before sending it.
3. [ ] Have OpenCode run the new example code and check its output.

# Agents

[Agents](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/agents) in OpenCode are configurable AI assistants with their own prompts, models, and permissions.

OpenCode ships with two built-in primary agents, "Build" and "Plan", but you can also _create your own_ with custom tools, model settings, instructions, etc.

For example, you might want a `review` agent that:

- Can read files and diffs, but can't edit
- Can't run any destructive shell commands
- Is pre-loaded with instructions to compare each change against a set of rules
- Won't ever run more than 6 agentic cycles without human input

> [!warning]
>

lessons.title: Temperature
lessons.readme:
# Temperature

Prompting matters, but model settings can matter too. If your agent acts too chaotic, too verbose, or too eager to wander off into weird ideas, the prompt itself might not be the problem.

Nearly all LLM providers support settings that control the model's behavior outside the prompt itself. One of the most common is "[temperature](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/llm-temperature)."

Lower temperature (closer to `0.0`) means:

- More focused responses
- Less randomness

Higher temperature (closer to `1.0`) means:

- More variety and "creativity" (scare quotes intended)
- Less control over the output

> [!dax]
>
> There are some developers who get really deep into knob-turning, which is why we expose these config options for them. But personally I don't really mess with temperature at all when coding.

## Don't Overtune

I know you think you've graduated from "Software Engineer" to "AI Engineer," but spending hours tweaking temperature is _not_ time well spent, especially when the next model update might completely change your favorite settings.

So, use the defaults unless you have a clear problem that's _best_ addressed by changing temperature.

Set temperature on the [provider, model, or variant](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/models#options). DeepSeek [ignores temperature in thinking mode](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/api/create-chat-completion/), so this model-level override for `DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free` also disables thinking:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "providers": {
    "opencode": {
      "models": {
        "deepseek-v4.1-flash-free": {
          "body": {
            "reasoning_effort": "none",
            "temperature": 0.1,
          },
        },
      },
    },
  },
}
```

> [!warning]
>
> These request fields depend on the provider, not every provider supports every setting.

## Assignment

**Compare Sloperator slogans at two temperatures.**

1. [ ] If your normal preferred model does _not_ allow temperature configuration, use one that does (like `opencode/deepseek-v4.1-flash-free`) instead.

   Tell OpenCode to update the `model` field in `opencode.jsonc` if needed; that needs to be set to a model that supports temperature.

2. [ ] Tell OpenCode to set your model's _model-level_ `body.temperature` to `0.9` in `opencode.jsonc`, using the example above.

   If you're using DeepSeek, also set `body.reasoning_effort` to `"none"` for this exercise.

3. [ ] Start a new OpenCode session, then ask the model to brainstorm five Sloperator slogans, and save them in `SLOGANS.md`.
4. [ ] Have the agent lower the model's temperature value to `0.1`.
5. [ ] Start yet another session, then ask for five more slogans, and save them in `SLOGANS.md` as well. Compare the responses.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

_After submitting, go back to your preferred model and default temperature. Also remove the `body.reasoning_effort` override, if you added it._

lessons.readme:
# Custom Agents

A custom agent can be defined easily with a Markdown file. And OpenCode watches for changes in its config directories, so if you update an agent's settings, it will _normally_ reload without a restart.

Put the file in one of these locations:

- `.opencode/agents/` for a project-specific agent
- `~/.config/opencode/agents/` for a global agent

For example, a file at `.opencode/agents/review.md` creates a `review` agent in the current project:

```md
---
description: Reviews code for bugs, regressions, and risky changes
mode: primary
permissions:
  - action: edit
    resource: "*"
    effect: deny
  - action: shell
    resource: "*"
    effect: deny
---

You are a code review agent. Focus on:

- Finding bugs and edge cases
- Explaining tradeoffs clearly
- Suggesting changes without making direct edits
- Code quality and best practices
- Performance implications
- Security concerns
```

There are two parts to the file:

- The **frontmatter** at the top _configures_ the agent.
- The **Markdown body** below that is the agent's _system prompt_.

The frontmatter fields in this example are:

- `description`: tells OpenCode and the model when this agent should be used
- `mode`: whether it's a `primary`, `subagent`, or `all` agent (we'll talk about subagents soon)
- `permissions`: controls what the agent can do and which resources it can act on

> [!tip]
>
> Create a custom primary agent when you need separate permissions, tools, or subagent access. A custom agent is overkill when all you need is a different system prompt.

## Assignment

**Create a read-only agent** for reviewing Sloperator.

1. [ ] In **Build** mode, tell OpenCode to create `.opencode/agents/review.md` as a new primary agent. Give it code-review instructions and permissions that deny all actions except `read`, `glob`, and `grep`.
2. [ ] Use [[Shift]]+[[Tab]] to switch to the **review** agent and tell it to review the division implementation and tests. Read its findings.
   > [!tip]
   >
   > If the new agent doesn't appear, use the `/reload` command to reload your configuration without restarting OpenCode.
3. [ ] Switch back to **Build**.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

lessons.title: Max Steps
lessons.readme:
# Max Steps

Sometimes you know a task _really just shouldn't take that long_.

You can limit your agent's ability to spin its wheels with the [`steps`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/agents#steps) setting. Each step is one _model response_, which can include multiple tool calls. The results of those calls feed into the next step.

If you set `steps: 5`, the agent gets at most five model steps. On the final step, OpenCode disables tool calls and asks the model to summarize. A new user prompt will reset the allowance.

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "agents": {
    "quick-thinker": {
      "description": "Fast reasoning with limited iterations",
      "system": "Solve problems with minimal steps.",
      "steps": 5,
    },
  },
}
```

> [!info]
>
> Agents can be specified in either [Markdown or JSON](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/agents#formats).

Frankly, you probably won't use this setting very often in day-to-day coding, but it can be very useful when you're building an automated pipeline that _uses_ an agent, with something like [`opencode run`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli#automation).

## Assignment

**Limit the review agent's steps** in one run.

1. [ ] In Build mode, tell OpenCode to set `steps: 2` in `.opencode/agents/review.md`.
2. [ ] Select **review** and tell it to inspect the lexer, parser, and evaluator in separate tool calls before reviewing their error handling. Watch how far it gets before summarizing.
3. [ ] Switch back to **Build**.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

lessons.title: Subagents
lessons.readme:
# Subagents

Subagents are specialized agents that your primary agent can spin off concurrently to tackle _narrower_ jobs. OpenCode ships with two [built-in subagents](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/agents#builtins):

- `general`: a general-purpose worker that can research and execute multi-step tasks
- `explore`: a fast, read-only worker for codebase and web exploration

## Why Bother?

The big advantage is **isolation**.

When a primary agent invokes a subagent, that work happens in a _child session_ instead of cluttering the context of the parent session with every search, command, and intermediate thought.

Subagents can also be _cost-efficient_ because the isolated session can use a **different model**. For example, you might want your `explore` subagent to use a small, cheap model for searching around the codebase, then summarize its findings and inject them back into the parent session for your expensive model to analyze.

They can also be **faster** because subagents can run in parallel. When it launches a subagent in the background, your primary agent can keep working and receive the result when it's ready. Foreground calls wait for the subagent to finish.

## How to Use Subagents

Subagents are _mostly_ called autonomously by your primary agent, just like any other tool. However, you can also invoke them manually with the `@` symbol:

```text
@explore go find all the files related to authentication and summarize their contents for me
```

> [!theo]
>
> I never call subagents explicitly (though my primary agent uses them invisibly, of course). Your mileage may vary.

## Assignment

Have a subagent **find a gap in Sloperator's lexer test coverage**.

1. [ ] Tell the primary Build agent to delegate a search to `explore` for a `LexicalError` missing a [regression test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regression_testing).
2. [ ] Inspect the child session's work and its summary. (You can click the subagent's name in the session to see its work. It's collapsed by default.)
3. [ ] Tell the primary Build agent to create `tests/test_lexer_regression.py` and add a test for the untested error.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

lessons.title: Task Permissions
lessons.readme:
# Task Permissions

Just because a subagent _exists_ doesn't mean every agent should be allowed to invoke it.

You can control that with [`subagent` permission rules](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/agents#permissions).

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "agents": {
    "orchestrator": {
      "mode": "primary",
      "permissions": [
        { "action": "subagent", "resource": "*", "effect": "deny" },
        {
          "action": "subagent",
          "resource": "orchestrator-*",
          "effect": "allow",
        },
        { "action": "subagent", "resource": "code-reviewer", "effect": "ask" },
      ],
    },
  },
}
```

These rules give the `orchestrator` agent the following behavior:

- `*` denies all subagent invocation by default
- `orchestrator-*` allows any subagent ID that starts with `orchestrator-`
- `code-reviewer` requires approval before the orchestrator can invoke that subagent

The exceptions work because OpenCode evaluates rules _in order_ and the last matching rule wins.

> [!tip]
>
> These rules only restrict what an _agent_ can invoke automatically. They do **not** stop _you_ from manually invoking a subagent directly through the UI.

## Assignment

**Block automatic delegation** to `explore`.

1. [ ] Tell OpenCode to append a project permission rule denying the `subagent` action for the `explore` resource.
2. [ ] Tell the primary Build agent to delegate a lexer search to `explore`, rather than invoking it yourself with `@explore`. Confirm that it _cannot_ launch the child agent.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

lessons.title: What Is Context?
lessons.readme:
# What Is Context?

**Context** is all the information your AI model can "see" when it's generating a response. A "[context window](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/context-window)" is the limit on how much of that information the model can work with at once.

![context](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/context-1920x1080.mp4)

Giving an agent the ability to read files, connect to a database, or call an API does _not_ automatically put that data in the model's context. The agent needs to _fetch_ it first. When the model is generating text, it uses the tokens in context to _predict the next token_, then repeats the process with the new token included.

![inference pipeline](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/u1trGAY-1280x664.png)

What makes AI _feel_ more sophisticated is that all the tool-calling, file-reading, etc. injects more information into context – often managed automatically by agents – _before_ the model generates its final response to a prompt.

## Why Not Just Say "Prompt"?

The prompt that you enter is only _part_ of the context, and with coding, usually a very small part. Context can include:

- System prompts
- Previous messages
- Reasoning tokens
- Tool calls and their results
- Your prompt (latest user message)

A context window of **1 million tokens** can hold roughly 750,000 words of English text, or about 1.5x the length of the entire _Lord of the Rings_ trilogy. That's _much_ more than you'd ever write into a prompt by hand, but not so much when you're trying to shove your entire codebase, documentation, and session history into the model's context.
