lessons.readme:
# Context As RAM

Just like [RAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random-access_memory) is the working memory of a computer, it's useful to think of a model's context window as its memory.

You wouldn't slow your computer down by [hoarding tabs](https://www.urbandictionary.com/define.php?term=Tab-Hoarder), _would_ you? Then why bloat your context window?

> [!theo]
>
> Or if you are a tab-hoarder like me, hopefully you at least understand it's not ideal.

## Managing Context in OpenCode

The "Context" section in OpenCode's right-hand sidebar shows your current context usage in _tokens_ and as a _percentage_ of your model's maximum.

When your agent goes about reading files, fetching data from the web, or using tools, it's storing _all that data_ (or sometimes a summary of it) in the context window. Remember how we talked about how each token prediction is a simple pipeline?

```text
input tokens -> model -> next token
```

Well, if your input is full of irrelevant information, not only will it make your inference _slower and more expensive_, it can also confuse the AI and make it more likely to generate a bad response.

> [!dax]
>
> Agents are pretty good at figuring out what files to load, what folders to look in, etc. Just make sure your prompt has as much relevant info as possible.

**When you're explaining a task to a coworker, you don't bring in the story of your latest failed romantic endeavor** (I hope). You just give them the details needed for the task at hand. That's also how you should treat your LLM's context.

## Assignment

# New Sessions

So managing context is super important, and luckily, you don't have to manually do much to keep your context sane.

90% of the time, all you need to do is ~~kill it with fire~~ _start a new session_. When your current session's context is getting too large, or more importantly, you're noticing that the model is referring back to old irrelevant instructions, assumptions, or data – just start fresh.

The `/new` command in OpenCode starts a fresh conversation without carrying over the previous session's history. Project instructions still apply, and your files stay as they are.

Don't worry, you can use the `/sessions` command to jump back and resume any previous session at any time. Or use the tabs along the top of the TUI.

> [!lane]
>
> Personally, I don't love the tabs, because I use tabs _within_ my terminal. If you want, you can disable them in `/settings`.

lessons.title: Token Economics
lessons.readme:
# Token Economics

Bloated context doesn't just cause problems for your model's performance, it can also hurt the ol' pocketbook. As we discussed earlier, AI usage is generally billed by the token (or by a subscription with token caps).

But generally speaking, more tokens mean more cost. And **larger context = more input tokens**.

## Accumulation

How is it even possible to use millions of tokens?!? Well, each agentic step can add tool calls and reasoning steps that you don't even see. So a few prompts can easily balloon into many tens of thousands of tokens underneath your conversation.

Also consider that each time you send a message, the LLM has to reprocess the entire conversation. It doesn't only process the new message like a human would. If your session already has 100,000 tokens in context, sending 10 more messages in that conversation means at least 1 million input tokens, even if no other tool calls are made.

![context window growth](courses/diagrams/5040cb38-46a4-4472-b199-365e0da8230e/token-economics.svg)

## Caching

To be fair, input tokens usually cost _far_ less than output tokens. And a significant percentage of [input tokens get cached](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching), which further reduces the cost.

Cache hits are not guaranteed, though, and cached tokens still occupy context space and cost money. For example, [Google's introductory input pricing for `gemini-4-argon`](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing) includes a 95% discount for cached tokens:

- $2.00 per million **uncached input tokens**
- $0.10 per million **cached input tokens**

The introductory period lasts through November 30, 2026. Starting December 1, uncached input rises to $4.00 and cached input to $0.20 per million tokens.

## Don't Shove Everything in Context

Not every session you start needs to have the entirety of your codebase, docs, and session history in context. That's why agent harnesses like OpenCode have tools for fetching files and data _on demand_. You can keep prompt templates, documentation, and instructions for tool calling _elsewhere_ (like in files on disk) and tell your model to go _read_ them as needed.

lessons.readme:
# Ignoring Files

A great way to bloat context is to let OpenCode read giant chunks of noisy, irrelevant files.

## Gitignore

OpenCode's content searches use [`ripgrep`](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep), which respects [`.gitignore`](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitignore) patterns by default. This keeps ordinary searches from getting blasted by `node_modules/` or `dist/` folders. That said, explicit file patterns _can_ override those exclusions, and the agent can still read ignored files directly if needed.

You don't really need anything AI-specific here. Just make sure you actually `.gitignore` generated files and dependencies like you normally would:

- Build output (`dist/`, `build/`, generated assets)
- Dependency trees (`node_modules/`, `.venv/`)
- Large logs and temporary dumps
- Binary blobs that won't help code reasoning

## Ignore

You might want OpenCode searches to _include_ a path covered by `.gitignore`, or to _exclude_ a path without changing which files Git tracks. To override `ripgrep`'s default search behavior, create a [`.ignore`](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/blob/master/GUIDE.md#automatic-filtering) file in your project root:

```gitignore
!dist/
fixtures/xl-dump.json
```

The `!` pattern _re-includes_ `dist/` in search results, while the regular pattern excludes `fixtures/xl-dump.json`.

Then tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

# File Watcher

OpenCode watches the filesystem for relevant changes, and those events let it reload watched skills and plugins while it's still running.

> [!warning]
>
> File-watching _cannot_ merge conflicting edits. OpenCode's edit tools use the current file contents and may fail when the text they expected has changed. Review the diff whenever you and an agent edit the same file.

The [`watcher.ignore`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/config#watcher) option in `opencode.jsonc` suppresses filesystem events for matching files and folders. This can reduce noise from frequently rebuilt artifacts; it doesn't stop the agent from searching or reading them:

```jsonc
{
  "watcher": {
    "ignore": ["node_modules/**", "dist/**", ".git/**"],
  },
}
```

> [!dax]
>
> I don't recommend messing with this option in _most_ of your projects unless you're specifically running into watcher-related issues.

## Assignment

lessons.title: Lost in the Middle
lessons.readme:
# Lost in the Middle

Having a large context window doesn't mean a model uses every part of it equally well. A famous study called "[Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)" found that models tend to retrieve information better from the _beginning_ and _end_ of long contexts, rather than from the middle.

Funny enough, AI is kinda like a human in this regard. ~~It's like it was trained on _human data_ or something...~~ Send your coworker a 3-page email, and they'll probably read the first 3 sentences and the last 3 sentences most thoroughly, skimming everything between.

## What This Means for Prompt Design

The effect varies by model and task, and retrieving facts isn't the same as following instructions. Still, it's a useful reminder: **don't bury the important stuff**.

This does _not_ mean that you can't have big prompts. You totally can! For longer prompts (and especially reusable prompt _templates_), just make sure the goal and the key constraints are as easy to find as possible. State them up front, and consider a short reminder at the end when there's a lot of supporting material in the middle.

## Assignment

lessons.title: Compaction
lessons.readme:
# Compaction

If you've never hit a context window limit using a "raw" AI provider's API, know that it's literally a hard stop. You just get an error saying the input is too long.

To avoid this, OpenCode (like other coding agents) will automatically _compact_ your session as you approach the context window limit. In practice, and assuming you're using a model with a reasonably large window, you'll likely never have a "hard stop" because OpenCode's auto-compaction will keep you in safe territory.

## How Compaction Works

Unlike lossless [compression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_compression), compaction doesn't let you reconstruct every detail from the shortened version of the context. It's [lossy](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/lossy): some information is concretely left out.

By default, OpenCode _asks the model to summarize_ the session's history and current state, retaining some recent context alongside the summary. Earlier messages remain saved on disk, but the model continues the session using the shorter context. The summary might contain:

- A list of relevant files and what matters about them
- A summary of the goal and what's been tried so far
- Constraints and decisions that should persist
- Suggested next steps

## Manual vs. Automatic

While compaction happens automatically as you approach the context window limit (you'll notice the TUI telling you that it's compacting), you can also trigger it manually at any time with the [`/compact`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/compaction#manual) command. Include instructions to guide the compaction.

> [!dax]
>
> Compaction used to suck, but now it's pretty good at retaining relevant context.
>
> Sometimes I manually `/compact` after a task is "roughly done," like where I might make a Git commit. Then I continue from there in the same session.
>
> I used to make new sessions all the time, but now I tend to have super long-running sessions with more compaction.

lessons.readme:
# Undo and Redo

I like to think of my session contexts more as "resources" than "conversations." They're ultimately logs of text, so it's easy to build tools for manipulating them. Just like `git` makes manipulating code changes super powerful, some agent session management tools can edit session context in ingenious ways.

The [`/undo` command](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/snapshots) rolls back the last _response_ the model gave you. If OpenCode captured a matching filesystem snapshot, it also **restores the files** changed by that response!

After running `/undo` and _before submitting another prompt_, you can use `/redo` to restore the conversation and files to the state that you just rolled back from. That said, submitting a new prompt makes the undo permanent, so you can no longer redo it!

OpenCode's snapshot capture requires a Git repository and is on a best-effort basis. `/undo` can't reverse all side effects of shell commands, e.g., changes to databases or files outside the working repo, effects on running processes, and network operations. So, it's a convenience, but not a replacement for good [Git hygiene and backups](https://about.gitlab.com/topics/version-control/version-control-best-practices/).

> [!dax]
>
> I actually use `/undo` quite a bit. If I get a "bad" output, and I can tell it was just a bad prompt, a quick undo + re-prompt is a lot faster than trying to explain to the AI what went wrong and how to get back on track.

## Assignment

Unary minus should reject a boolean, so this SlopLang program should produce a runtime error (the ✅ emoji is `true` in SlopLang):

```slop

```

While this is okay:

```slop

```

2. [ ] Use `/undo` and inspect the files to confirm that the test addition was reverted.
3. [ ] _Before sending another prompt_, use `/redo` and confirm the test returns.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

# Forking

Another powerful context-manipulation command is `/fork`. It creates a _new session_ with the same context as the current session – while also letting you quickly choose a "fork point" from the recent message history.

Sometimes I want to try a different approach, but I don't want to recreate all the context and history of my current session from scratch. I just fork off the latest message that has the context I actually want, and keep going in the new session.

1. Branch to try a risky idea.
2. Keep the main session clean.
3. Return to the main session if the experiment fails.

The fork separates the conversation, but **both sessions share the same working directory**. Returning to the original session does _not_ undo file changes made in the fork... that said, you can always `/fork` and instruct the model to copy the files into a new worktree.

## Assignment

This SlopLang program passes the result of `add(1, 2)` to `hallucinate`:

```slop
clanker add(left, right) {
    ship left + right✨
}
hallucinate(add(1, 2))✨
```

So it should print `3`, and the parser should recognize the inner call `add(1,2)` as an argument to the outer call `hallucinate()`. But the current tests don't cover this case, so **add a new parser test in a forked session**.

1. [ ] Use `/fork` to branch from your current session. If you're in a brand-new session, `/fork` won't be available because _there's nothing to fork yet_.
2. [ ] In the fork, tell OpenCode to add a `tests/test_nested_calls.py` file with a new test covering a call used directly as an argument to another call.
3. [ ] Return to the original session with `/sessions`. Confirm that the fork's conversation is separate, while its test file is visible in the shared working directory.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

lessons.title: Secrets in Context
lessons.readme:
# Secrets in Context

Anything you put in an OpenCode session _can_ become part of the model's context. That includes pasted text, file contents, and shell output. Copying or exporting the session can spread that information further.

So yes, developer secrets (passwords, API keys, tokens, etc.) can leak into "context" in many ways, not _just_ through committed code.

## Why Are Secrets in Context Bad?

Even if your provider doesn't use your data for training, putting secrets in context still _sends_ them to that provider. Giving a remote model access to your plain-text secrets is a BIG risk and should **absolutely be avoided**.

Now, if you're running a model _locally on your own hardware_, the risk is much lower because at least the secret isn't leaving your machine. But even then, you should be careful about what secrets you put into context: you might accidentally _reuse_ that session later with a different model. Also, your session history gets saved on disk, so if a session includes a plain-text secret, now there's another copy of it to worry about.

## The Good News

OpenCode's [default permissions](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/permissions#defaults) allow `read` for most files, but `.env` files ask for your approval by default.

The `shell` tool runs with your user's host permissions, so **treat shell access as real terminal access**, not as a filesystem sandbox.

## The Bad News

Not all secrets are in `.env` files. You can still leak secrets by:

- Pasting API keys directly into the chat
- Approving a shell command that prints secret values
- Letting logs dump authentication tokens into the terminal
- Allowing OpenCode to run a script that accesses other parts of the filesystem
- Copying or exporting a contaminated session into another system

## Best Practices

Tune your permissions to deny reads of files you use for secrets, or require explicit approval. For example, this rule in `opencode.jsonc` blocks the `read` tool from opening `.secrets` files:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "read", "resource": "*.secrets", "effect": "deny" },
  ],
}
```

And just _be careful_. No single list can cover all the potential ways to leak secrets into context. If you notice a risk of leaking secrets in one of your projects, make a change to your workflow.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Tell OpenCode to append a permission rule denying `read` for `*.env` in `opencode.jsonc`.
2. [ ] Tell it to read `.env` with the `read` tool. Confirm that access is denied.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

lessons.readme:
# AGENTS.md

It gets _super tiresome_ to give the **same** instructions to your agent every time you start a new session.

The good news is you can keep your project-specific instructions in an [`AGENTS.md`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/instructions) file so you don't need to copy and paste them every time!

![AGENTS.md rules explainer](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/agents-md-rules_1920x1080-1920x1080.mp4)

## Where It Lives

OpenCode automatically looks for `AGENTS.md` in two places:

- **Project-level:** OpenCode starts from your current working directory and walks _up_ to your home directory. If your project is outside of your home directory, the search stops at the project root instead. So, if you start OpenCode in `~/project/src/` and have a `~/project/src/AGENTS.md` file and another at the project root `~/project/AGENTS.md`, _both get loaded_.
- **Global:** at `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`. This is for _personal_ defaults you want across _all your projects_ (like "Always leave changes unstaged for my review" or "You can find examples of my writing style in `~/prose`").

Project-level rules and global rules are **combined**, not replaced. The agent sees **all** of them.

> [!tip]
>
> Most agents (even Claude, finally) support `AGENTS.md`, but many also have their own agent-specific instructions files, like `CLAUDE.md`. Same exact idea, different filename.

## Example

In true dog-fooding form, the OpenCode team uses OpenCode to build OpenCode, and [the OpenCode repo](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode) is an S-tier example of how to use `AGENTS.md` files. Review an excerpt from their [project-level `AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/6baad7fc3e15e1ff5859f43de62892052d4e6c32/AGENTS.md) in the "Tip" section at the bottom of this page.

> [!lane]
>
> I like to write bullet-point-style rules, but then also list concrete **examples** of "good" and "bad" code that illustrate the rules. The more specific you can be, the better the agent will comply.

## Assignment

Generate Sloperator's project instructions.

1. [ ] Run `/init` in OpenCode to create a new `AGENTS.md` file in the project root.
2. [ ] Read the resulting `AGENTS.md`. Tell OpenCode to correct any inaccurate commands or project details you find, then hand-edit the file to your liking.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

## Tip

At the time of writing, this is a shortened excerpt from the [project-level `AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/6baad7fc3e15e1ff5859f43de62892052d4e6c32/AGENTS.md) in the OpenCode repo.

````md
- After changing the public Protocol or Server `HttpApi`, run `bun run generate` from `packages/client`. Do not edit generated client files directly.
- Keep runtime dependencies directed from Schema to Core and Protocol, then from Core and Protocol to Server. Client runtime code may depend on Schema and Protocol but never Core or Server; `sdk-next` composes Client, Core, and Server.
- The default branch in this repo is `v2`.
- Base all new branches and worktrees on `v2`, or `origin/v2` when the local `v2` ref is unavailable. Do not base them on `dev`.
- Local `main` ref may not exist; use `v2` or `origin/v2` for diffs.

## Branch Names

Use a short branch name of at most three words, separated by hyphens. Do not use slashes or type prefixes like `feat/` or `fix/`.

Examples: `session-recovery`, `fix-scroll-state`, `regenerate-sdk`.

## Style Guide

### General Principles

- Keep things in one function unless composable or reusable
- Avoid `try`/`catch` where possible
- Avoid using the `any` type
- Use Bun APIs when possible, like `Bun.file()`
- Rely on type inference when possible; avoid explicit type annotations or interfaces unless necessary for exports or clarity
- Prefer functional array methods (flatMap, filter, map) over for loops; use type guards on filter to maintain type inference downstream

```ts
// Good
const journal = await Bun.file(path.join(dir, "journal.json")).json();

// Bad
const journalPath = path.join(dir, "journal.json");
const journal = await Bun.file(journalPath).json();
```

## Testing

- Avoid mocks as much as possible, you shouldn't be using globalThis.\* at all unless it's the only option.
- Test actual implementation, do not duplicate logic into tests
- Tests cannot run from repo root (guard: `do-not-run-tests-from-root`); run from package directories like `packages/core`.

## Type Checking

- Always run `bun typecheck` from package directories (for example, `packages/core`), never `tsc` directly.
````

# Rule Precedence

In a large project, you might store agent rules in several places:

- A repo-root `AGENTS.md`
- A nested `AGENTS.md` in a subdirectory for a specific package
- A global `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md` on your machine

Those rules are **all combined** into your agent's context window. OpenCode doesn't throw out one set of rules just because another exists.

## Nested AGENTS.md Files

You can put `AGENTS.md` files in _subdirectories_ within your project, and they'll be loaded **dynamically** when the agent reads files in that directory. Say you have a monorepo with the following rules files:

```text
AGENTS.md               # root-level rules
packages/api/AGENTS.md  # API-specific rules
packages/web/AGENTS.md  # web-specific rules
```

The root `AGENTS.md` is always part of the initial instructions, but OpenCode only loads `packages/api/AGENTS.md` once the agent successfully reads a file or lists a directory inside `packages/api/`. It then adds those rules to the session once and keeps them for the rest of the conversation.

> [!lane]
>
> We have a monorepo at Boot.dev, and we use nested `AGENTS.md` files for our frontend, backend, and course content directories. No sense injecting a bunch of frontend-specific rules into context when a session only cares about backend code.

lessons.readme:
# Writing an AGENTS.md

Writing a _good_ `AGENTS.md` is simple, but not easy. A good rules file _will_ differ from any "prompt template" you've seen online because every team, project, and domain is different.

## Goal

The real _goal_ of the `AGENTS.md` file is to save yourself from having to _retype_ the same information into each new session. So at the end of the day, the most important criterion for deciding what goes into it is:

> "What do I want to tell the agent every time I start a new session?"

So, let's go over common sections your `AGENTS.md` might have, and what to include in them.

## Style Guide

Include code patterns that you _do_ and _don't_ like. As you're coding with AI, whenever you notice it writing code you don't like, fix it, but also tell it to update this section with the example. A brief explanation and an example are perfect.

````md
- Avoid unnecessary destructuring. Use dot notation to preserve context.

```ts
// Good
obj.a;
obj.b;

// Bad
const { a, b } = obj;
```
````

## Testing Guide

This section should include _how_ and _when_ to write tests, but also any instructions about how to run them, and how to set up dependencies if there are any.

```md
- Avoid using mocks to the extent possible. Refactor functions to make business logic more easily testable without them.
- Use `go test` to run tests, but only test the specific function you're working on when iterating; our test suite is large.
```

## Database Schema

Depending on your project's setup, it might be simple enough to point the agent at your migration files or ORM models to give it an understanding of the schema. If your schema lives outside the codebase, I'd recommend finding _some_ way to make it easily accessible to the agent, and telling the agent how to find it here.

## Project Structure

Give a _very_ high-level overview of the repo so the agent knows where to look for things.

```md
- `cmd/` – CLI entrypoints
- `internal/api/` – HTTP handlers
- `internal/store/` – Database layer (PostgreSQL)
- `migrations/` – SQL migration files
```

> [!danger]
>
> Be careful about being _too_ detailed here. The agent is really good at traversing file trees, and an out-of-date summary is worse than none at all. That said, it can save "startup" time in new sessions by not forcing the agent to relearn the structure.

## Git Workflow

This section _may_ live in the project repo, but it may also be a better fit in your personal (global) `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md` if it contains _personal_ preferences rather than _team_ preferences. It should explain how you want your agent to interact with Git (if at all) when making a change. For example, I use this:

```md
- Never assume that you should stage or commit a change unless I ask you to. I like to review your changes unstaged.
- When I ask you to commit and push, push to a new feature branch (not `main`) if you aren't already on one.
- Rebase off of the `main` branch before pushing, unless I ask for something else.
- Look at the `git log` after rebasing. If there are any sloppy "wip" or "fixup" commits, squash them into the most logical commit message before pushing.
- Use short, single-sentence conventional commit messages.
- Never create a pull request without being asked to.
```

## Tools / Scripts

We'll talk more about some alternative strategies for tools and scripts later, but if you have some that you want your agent to use on a _very_ regular basis, it makes sense to list them here.

For example, at Boot.dev, we have a custom script that formats the Markdown files of our lessons in a specific way, and we point it out to the LLM here.

## What to Leave Out

- Don't duplicate what's already in your `README.md` or other documentation. Just tell your agent where to find those files if they're needed.
- Don't be redundant; state each rule once with just one or two examples.
- Don't put secrets or credentials in here (duh). This file should be committed.
- Omit anything that the base model likely _already knows_. You don't need to re-teach it how to write Python code, for example.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

# AGENTS vs. README

Should you put your project info in `AGENTS.md` or `README.md`?

The answer is "both"... but please **don't repeat yourself**. The files can simply _reference_ each other!

## README Is for Humans

Your `README.md` is documentation for _humans_. Sometimes that's other maintainers, but sometimes it's just users! In many projects it doubles as a landing page on GitHub.

It can be long, include narrative, have badges, screenshots, installation steps, a changelog link – whatever humans want to know at a glance about the project.

An agent _can_ read it, but you should only _instruct_ it to read it on an as-needed basis.

## AGENTS Is for Clankers

`AGENTS.md` is loaded into the system prompt in _every single session_. Every token in it has a recurring cost, and it competes with your actual prompt for attention, so keep it _tightly scoped_.

| Content                                        | README | AGENTS | Other         |
| ---------------------------------------------- | :----: | :----: | ------------- |
| "Always use `slog`, never `fmt.Println`"       |        |   X    |               |
| "Run tests with `go test ./...`"               |        |   X    |               |
| "NEVER USE `.then` OVER `await` YOU CRAZY BOT" |        |   X    |               |
| Setup instructions for new human devs          |   X    |        |               |
| "To install this program locally..."           |   X    |        |               |
| API endpoint documentation                     |        |        | `docs/api.md` |

lessons.readme:
# Updating Rules

An out-of-date `AGENTS.md` is _worse_ than no `AGENTS.md` at all.

Stale rules **actively mislead** the agent. For example, if your rules say "use the `users` table," but you renamed it to `accounts`, the agent might confidently write queries against a table that doesn't exist (at least, until the tests fail). Worse, it would have _discovered_ the correct name right off the bat if you simply didn't have a bad `AGENTS.md` file.

## Update Often

Update your `AGENTS.md` whenever you:

- Rename or restructure important directories
- Change your test/lint/build commands
- Add or remove major dependencies
- Establish a new convention (or retire an old one)
- **Notice the agent repeatedly doing something wrong**

> [!tip]
>
> As models improve, revisit your rules and remove instructions that are no longer useful... the models are getting smarter over time and need less hand-holding.

## Let the Bot Update Itself

I have a line in my _personal_ `AGENTS.md` that says:

> [!lane]
>
> When I ask you to undo an AI-written change, and the mistake isn't obvious or already covered in `AGENTS.md`, suggest an `AGENTS.md` edit to prevent the same problem. Always ask permission before making the edit.

This helps the bot remind me to keep my rules files up to date. Quite often the suggested edit needs a bit of work, but it has at least gotten me in a better habit of documenting my preferences.

# Feedback Loops

AI agents are ~~not completely useless~~ better when they can get fast, accurate, and **automated** feedback about their work. A feedback loop is simple:

1. Attempt a change
2. Run a check
3. Inspect the results of the check
4. Repeat

![feedback loops](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/feedback-loops-1920x1080.mp4)

Humans do best with tight feedback loops as well, but it's even _more_ important for AI because if the checks are good, the AI can get pretty dang far without needing to be babysat the whole way. Examples of "checks" include:

- Unit tests (or integration and even end-to-end tests)
- Formatters
- Linters
- Type checkers
- Compilers

Great feedback loops do two things:

1. **Catch bad changes quickly** (before the agent builds on top of them)
2. **Give the agent precise feedback** about what failed so it can make a fix without guessing

## Assignment

**Add support for `!`**, SlopLang's "not" operator. This code:

```slop
hallucinate(!✅, !❌, !!✅)✨
```

should print `❌ ✅ ✅`. The `!` operator flips a boolean, and using it twice flips it back. Currently, Sloperator doesn't support it. Using `!` on a number or string should produce a SlopLang runtime error.

1. [ ] Tell OpenCode to add the behavior above, along with tests and an update to `docs/spec.md`.
2. [ ] Tell it to run the ruff formatter, and if formatting changes are needed, tell it to fix them and rerun the check.

> [!tip]
>
> Agents are pretty smart at determining the next steps. My agent often does the ruff formatting without my mentioning formatting in the prompt.

# Static Typing

Personally, I'm a _big_ fan of statically typed languages. With AI coding, the value of static types becomes even more, well, _valuable_. Static analysis can immediately tell the model that it:

- Called a function with the wrong arguments
- Returned a value of the wrong type from a function
- Accessed a field that doesn't exist
- Broke an interface contract somewhere downstream

Most importantly, the model can learn these things _quickly_, before it actually runs the code. Types act as guardrails that catch the agent's mistakes the _instant_ they happen, rather than letting bad assumptions compound across a dozen files. Which, as we all know, can cost quite a bit of time and money in this token-hungry world.

> [!theo]
>
> So, Lane, when can we make a Rust course? Surely that must be among the best languages for AI agents!

> [!lane]
>
> ...soon™

```slop

```

prints `3 ✅`, then a blank line. Sloperator calculates the arguments before passing them to `hallucinate`, so it receives the number `3` and the boolean `✅`, not the text `1 + 2`.

Currently, built-in functions receive those values in a Python list. We want them to receive a tuple instead, so they can't add, remove, or replace arguments. **SlopLang's behavior should stay the same.**

# Automatic Formatting

Without a strict formatter, your agent will spend tokens worrying about indentation, trailing commas, and line length. Not only will it waste tokens, but it will also (like any human) be inconsistent.

So, just like when working with humans, always add a _code formatter_ to your workflow and put the problem to rest. For example:

- [oxfmt](https://oxc.rs/docs/guide/usage/formatter.html) for JavaScript/TypeScript, HTML, CSS, Markdown, and more
- [ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/) for Python
- [gofmt](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/gofmt) for Go

It's just one less thing for your agent to worry about.

> [!lane]
>
> I prompt my agent to make formatting changes _only_ as a _last step_, after all the logic changes are done. If I don't, I've found it can really slow things down.

> [!dax]
>
> I think the models are pretty good now at realizing that they're approaching the end of their work, and they'll call things like type checking and formatting on their own. If they don't, steer them in `AGENTS.md`.

Notably, adding empty strings doesn't change the original string, and adding a string with an emoji works as expected.

# Tests

Linters and type checks tell the agent whether the code is _structurally_ valid. Tests tell it whether the code _does the right thing_. There are two types of tests, generally speaking:

- [**Unit tests**](https://dave.cheney.net/2019/05/07/prefer-table-driven-tests) for fast, local correctness checks
- [**Integration tests**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integration_testing) for realistic end-to-end behavior

If your agent keeps "fixing" one bug while creating another, that's a strong signal that your test coverage is too thin or your test loop is too slow. When the agent can run `go test ./...` or `pytest` after every change and get an immediate pass/fail, it self-corrects _much_ more reliably.

lessons.title: AI and Test Economics
lessons.readme:
# AI and Test Economics

Writing tests with AI is _way_ cheaper than writing them by hand, which changes the ol' "How many tests are enough tests" debate in an interesting way.

These days, you can be more aggressive about adding targeted tests because the cost of writing them has come down. But "cheap to write" does **not** mean "generate 1,000 brittle, low-quality tests."

> [!dax]
>
> Good tests communicate _expected behavior_. You still don't want redundant, brittle, or meaningless tests just because someone told you 100% test coverage is a "best practice."
>
> That said, if there's undertested code that's been running correctly and _deserves_ to be covered by tests, it's great to get the agent to help you increase the test coverage.

## Should I Keep AI-Written Tests?

I've had people ask me:

> "My agent makes a lot of new tests for each change. Should I commit them all? Or let the agent discard them after it ensures the code works?"

Some developers assume that _all correct tests_ are _keepers_. But I actually have a higher standard:

- If I'm confident that the current expected behavior of the code _will be around long-term_, I **keep** tests. Good tests help prevent regressions.
- If the behavior _is likely to change_ as the code is refactored, extended, or deleted, or as business logic changes, then I'll **discard** those tests after validating that the code works. Less code to maintain and change later.

I do this because I don't want thousands of tests for specific behavior that _happens_ to be correct now, but that will likely get _respecified_ later. For example:

- A function that extracts email addresses from PDF files will likely _always_ do that, and keeping tests for that **saves me work later**.
- A function that sends a specific greeting message to new Discord users is very likely to _change_ as the marketing team experiments with different messaging, so keeping tests for that **creates more work later**.

# Skills

A ["skill"](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/skills) is (mostly) just a reusable prompt for an agent.

Skills are simple, but they're useful enough to deserve serious attention. They sit in the sweet spot between "type the same giant prompt again" and "stuff every possible instruction into `AGENTS.md` forever."

## Why Skills Exist

The problem with typing a new hyper-detailed prompt is the fundamental problem all AI aims to solve: _we're lazy af and don't like to type_.

The problem with using `AGENTS.md` and other documentation for _all_ your reusable prompts is that there are a lot of prompts you'll want to reuse _often_, but not in **literally every session**.

> Skills are prompts that you reuse frequently, but not in _every_ session.

A skill is a directory with a Markdown file and optional additional assets, like scripts or other resources. The agent can load the skill automatically, or you can load it manually. For example, I have a `talk-to-database` skill. It tells the agent how to connect to my production database safely (and in read-only mode) so that it can answer questions about the data without having to re-explain all the steps specific to my setup each time.

lessons.readme:
# Writing Skills

Again, a skill is just a directory with a Markdown file that has [YAML](https://yaml.org/) frontmatter at the top. Here's an example from the OpenCode maintainers:

```md
---
name: pull-request
description: Finalize approved changes into a pull request by adding, committing, rebasing, squashing, and drafting a new pull request
---

## Checklist

1. Run the CI steps locally to ensure everything passes. If it doesn't, inform the developer.
2. Stage and commit the approved changes.
   1. If there are any sloppy "wip," "fixup," or "draft" commits, squash them into the previous most logical commit.
3. Rebase onto `main`.
4. Create a draft pull request:
   1. Check if an open PR already exists.
   2. If no open PR exists yet, open a new one.
   3. If a PR already exists, update the existing branch and PR.
   4. If the branch history was rewritten locally, push with `--force-with-lease` when updating the PR.
   5. Use this format for the title: `[ticket number] - [short description of the change]`
   6. Include a more detailed description in the body, preferring single sentence bullet points.
      1. If the work is related to a GH issue, link it in this format: `related to #1234`
      2. If the work fully resolves a GH issue, link it in this format: `resolves #1234`

## Rules

- NEVER push direct to `main`
- Sign off all PR bodies with "pr drafted by ai slop cannon"
```

## Where Skills Live

- **Project-specific skills:** `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`
- **Global (personal) skills:** `~/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`

The directory name determines the skill's ID; its frontmatter `name` is just a display label, so keep them the same unless you enjoy creating confusion for yourself.

> [!warning]
>
> We'll use `.agents/skills` because multiple coding agents understand it. OpenCode's native location is `.opencode/skills`, and it also discovers `.claude/skills` for compatibility reasons.

## Invoking Skills

A skill at `.agents/skills/pull-request/SKILL.md` becomes `@pull-request`. Invoking it loads the skill's Markdown content into the conversation. You can also use `/skills` to open a searchable list of skills if you can't remember the exact name.

## Assignment

# Skills Are Tools

[Skills](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/skills) aren't _just_ manually invocable Markdown files. OpenCode also exposes them through the native `skill` tool.

That means your agent can see which skills are available and choose one automatically when it fits the task.

You might be thinking, "Wait, aren't skills literally just a tool that returns a hard-coded string?"

Well... mostly yes. I mean, the skill directory can contain scripts and other files related to the prompt, but it's not much more than that.

> [!dax]
>
> Some people think there's going to be this global database of skills that we'll all download from. I think there's mostly just two kinds of useful skills:
>
> - Skills you and your team write that are hyper-specific to your project and workflow
> - Skills that are published alongside a library or API so that users of those products can give their agents instructions for how to use them more effectively.
>
> Good skills are _specific_, not generalized "magic prompts".

lessons.readme:
# Skill Permissions

Just like tools, skill permissions can be controlled via [`opencode.jsonc`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/skills#permissions):

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "skill", "resource": "*", "effect": "allow" },
    { "action": "skill", "resource": "internal-*", "effect": "deny" },
    { "action": "skill", "resource": "experimental-*", "effect": "ask" },
  ],
}
```

The modes are the same, and wildcard rules work the same way:

- `allow`: the skill loads immediately
- `ask`: OpenCode asks before loading it
- `deny`: the skill is hidden from the agent and inaccessible to it

You can also give one agent its own skill rules:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "agents": {
    "plan": {
      "permissions": [
        { "action": "skill", "resource": "*", "effect": "deny" },
        { "action": "skill", "resource": "internal-*", "effect": "allow" },
      ],
    },
  },
}
```

Rules are ordered, so the narrower `internal-*` allow wins because it comes _after_ the wildcard deny.

lessons.readme:
# Composable Skills

The best skills are small and narrow enough that they're useful for many different types of tasks.

Try to follow the time-tested [Unix philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_philosophy) of "do one thing and do it well." If you have a massive skill, consider _breaking it up_ into a few more reusable ones.

Bad:

- `cracked-engineer-god-mode`

Better:

- `run-ci`
- `connect-to-database`
- `pr-review`

To give a more concrete example, I _could_ create a `gitstuff` skill that goes like this:

```md
1. Review the current working directory for any changes, and call attention to any issues.
2. If there are no issues, stage the changes.
3. Commit the changes with a conventional commit message, no more than one sentence long.
4. Rebase onto `main`, resolve any conflicts, and squash all my commits into one.
5. Push to a new feature branch in the format `myname_three_word_description`.
6. Create a draft pull request with the same name as the branch, and a body that includes a bullet point list of the changes, and any relevant issue links.
7. Sign off the PR body with `pr drafted by ai slop cannon`.
8. Request a review from Allan (he has nothing better to do).
```

Or I could break this up into a few smaller skills:

- `review` – Reviews the current working directory for any changes, and calls attention to any issues
- `commit` – Stages and commits changes with a conventional commit message, no more than one sentence long
- `sync` – Rebases the current branch onto `main`, resolves conflicts, and squashes
- `publish` – Pushes to the feature branch and creates a PR for Allan

Now if I (or my agent) want to use one _part_ of the workflow, we can. And the best part is, I can **still make the full skill as well**. But I don't rewrite the same instructions, just have a high-level skill that _references_ the smaller skills in order!

# Skill, Tool, or Agent?

Skills, tools, and agents all _feel_ like "things that do stuff," which makes it hard to know which is best for a given task that you're trying to automate. Here's how I think about it.

1. Is it mostly custom _code_ with defined inputs and outputs? **It's a tool.**
2. Is it a mostly a custom _prompt_ with some optional assets on disk? **It's a skill.**
3. Is it a "mode of operation" that _uses tools and skills_ with a specific set of _permissions and settings_? **It's an agent.**

The reality is that there usually isn't just one right answer. There's more than one way to ~~build a clanker~~ skin a cat.

From "smallest" to "largest", in terms of how much code and prompting is involved, I typically think of them like this:

1. Tools
2. Skills
3. Agents

# Custom Commands

[Custom commands](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/commands) and [skills](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/skills) are _very_ similar.

Both are basically reusable prompt templates. Both help you avoid retyping the same instructions. Both can live at the project level or globally.

But there _are_ a couple of important differences.

- A skill is exposed through OpenCode's native `skill` tool, meaning it's in context and can be loaded when the agent chooses to.
- A command is primarily a **user-invoked TUI shortcut**.

You run a command directly with a slash, like:

```text
/review-changes
```

- If you want something _the agent can proactively choose_ because it's semantically relevant, that's usually a **skill**.
- If you want a fast manual shortcut that _only you_ trigger, that's usually a **command**.

# Dynamic Prompts

OpenCode's command pipeline supports a few useful prompt features:

- Positional arguments like `$1`, `$2`, and `$ARGUMENTS`
- Shell output injection like ``!`bun test` ``

These are **command** features. Invoking a skill with `@skill-id` activates the skill body without parsing command arguments or shell blocks (but it's still valid to invoke a skill and provide additional instructions in the same prompt).

For example, a file at `.opencode/commands/linusfunc.md` could contain:

```md
---
description: Builds a function like Linus Torvalds would
---

Write a new function, complete with tests the way Linus Torvalds would. The function is $ARGUMENTS
```

The `$ARGUMENTS` variable is replaced by whatever you type after the command:

```text
/linusfunc a sum function that adds two numbers together
```

You can also break the arguments into separate positional variables if you like:

```text
The function is $1
It should $2 include tests
```

```text
/linusfunc sum not
```

Which produces this prompt:

```text
The function is sum
It should not include tests
```

## File References

While using `@path-to-file` works in the OpenCode prompt box to select a file and include its contents, it _doesn't_ work in a command prompt: it just stays plain text. Instead, just tell the agent to read the file:

```md
Read `src/asteroid.py`, then make me a new asteroid with jaggier edges.
```

Have the agent check for an existing Sloperator server before starting `uv run playground/server.py <port>` in the background. Keep the port argument outside the shell-injection block.

# MCP

[MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/getting-started/intro), or **Model Context Protocol**, is an open standard for systems (usually web APIs, but not necessarily) to expose tools, prompts, and data to AI agents.

That means an MCP server can give your agent access to things like:

- Issue trackers
- External docs
- Databases
- Internal APIs

![MCP diagram](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/goxChws-1280x636.png)

While yes, you _could_ just expose a REST API and a publicly hosted `SKILL` file and call it a day, MCP was actually released _before_ SKILLs, and it's a more tight-knit integration than just "here's some docs and an API, good luck with `curl`."

An MCP server is _not just a prompt_. It's more like an **external tool provider**. So instead of having to write 17 custom tools to integrate with the Stripe API, Stripe exposes a publicly hosted MCP server. You connect to it once, and you get [all those tools](https://docs.stripe.com/mcp?agent=none#tools) through a standardized interface.

## Architecture

[MCP's architecture](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture) is pretty interesting. It certainly got rolled out in a big hurry and it hasn't been without its critiques. However, it was [revised](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/) and has gained a lot of adoption and, as such, is likely here to stay.

There are three main components to an MCP system:

- **MCP Host:** The AI application that coordinates and manages one or multiple MCP clients
- **MCP Client:** A component that maintains a connection to an MCP server and obtains context from the server for the MCP host to use
- **MCP Server:** A program that provides context to MCP clients

As a user, the "MCP Host" and "MCP Client" kinda feel like the same thing. For example, in OpenCode, OpenCode itself is the "MCP Host", and as you add new MCP server connections, OpenCode creates a new dedicated "MCP Client" for each one.

## Communication Protocol

MCP servers can run [locally or remotely](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture#transport-layer). For local connections, [`stdio`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_streams) _direct process_ transport is used for maximum performance. For remote connections, [streamable HTTP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/streamable-http) is used.

As far as the actual [data format](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture#data-layer) being sent on those transports, MCP uses [JSON-RPC 2.0](https://www.jsonrpc.org/). It's a simple JSON-based protocol that feels more like function calls than an HTTP "REST" API.

lessons.title: Code Mode
lessons.readme:
# Code Mode

When presented with too many tools, models can [struggle](https://blog.cloudflare.com/code-mode/#whats-wrong-with-this) with calling the right tool or calling it correctly.

One thing models _are_ trained to do is write code. [Code Mode](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/tree/v2/packages/codemode#opencodecodemode) bridges what models do really well, and what MCP does well. It exposes tools through a JavaScript API so the model can [`execute`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/tools/#execute) code to search for tools, call tools, and process the results.

## Compose Tool Calls

With the [GitHub MCP server](https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server), an agent could generate:

```js
const issuePage = await tools.github.list_issues({
  owner: "anomalyco",
  repo: "opencode",
  state: "OPEN",
  orderBy: "CREATED_AT",
  direction: "DESC",
  perPage: 20,
  fields: ["number", "title", "assignees"],
});

return issuePage.issues
  .filter((issue) => !issue.assignees?.length)
  .map((issue) => ({
    number: issue.number,
    title: issue.title,
  }));
```

This example demonstrates an API tool call and programmatically processing the result. The result is way smaller yet so much more _relevant_.

Code Mode isn't limited to MCPs. It can run built-in and plugin tools.

## Deferred Discovery

OpenCode routes MCP tools through Code Mode by default. It shows the model a _limited catalog_, then lets it _discover_ additional tool signatures using the `search` function inside `execute`. Instead of dumping an MCP's entire list of tools into context, the model can use Code Mode to filter for relevant tools when needed.

## Disabling Code Mode

You can disable Code Mode in an MCP server's configuration. Only set [`codemode: false`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/mcp-servers/#permissions) for an MCP server when the provider _needs_ to see its tools in its native tool list.

## Assignment

**Fix the bug reported in the `bootdotdev/learn-ai-coding-starter` repository's GitHub issue.**

SlopLang allows variable names like `score2`, but this program currently fails with a syntax error:

```slop
slop score2 = 40✨
score2 = score2 + 2✨
hallucinate(score2)✨
```

It should create a `score2` variable set to `40`, add `2` to its value, and then print `42`. Names can _contain_ digits; they just can't _start_ with them.

1. [ ] Tell OpenCode to use Context7 to look up how to fetch issues with GitHub's REST API.
2. [ ] Have it fetch all of the starter repo's issues created by `theodore-s-beers` and find the variable-naming bug.
3. [ ] Tell it to fix the behavior described by the issue and add regression tests.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

lessons.title: Context Bloat
lessons.readme:
# Context Bloat

MCP servers can be useful, but just like everything in LLMs: **tool bloat becomes context bloat**.

Once you configure an MCP server, OpenCode has to describe its tools to the model. That catalog eats context whether the model calls a tool or not. _Disable servers you're not using._

> [!dax]
>
> The OpenCode team uses very few MCPs. I'm sure they can be useful occasionally, but you shouldn't add _all_ the integrations that you might possibly ever use. If your agent needs a tool, add it, but too many tools can actually confuse the models.

> [!lane]
>
> I have 2 active MCPs, and neither of them is shared across the team. One connects to PostHog so that my agent can read product metrics, and one connects to our marketing tool's API so I can ask it about budgets.

## Disable a Server

Luckily, it's super easy to disable an MCP server:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "context7": {
        "type": "remote",
        "url": "https://mcp.context7.com/mcp",
        "disabled": true,
      },
    },
  },
}
```

Setting [`disabled: true`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/mcp-servers#config) keeps the configuration but prevents OpenCode from connecting.

## Deny Individual Tools

You can also disable individual tools exposed by an MCP server by adding a [permission rule](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/mcp-servers#permissions):

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "context7_query-docs", "resource": "*", "effect": "deny" },
  ],
}
```

MCP tool actions use the format `<mcp-name>_<tool-name>`. OpenCode normalizes unsupported characters to underscores. If you need the exact name, literally just ask your agent! The catalog is already in its context.

> "List all tool names currently available to you, one per line."

## Assignment

**Disable Notion while keeping Context7 available.**

1. [ ] Ask OpenCode to list the available Context7 and Notion tools.
2. [ ] Tell it to disable the project's `notion` server without removing its configuration or disabling Context7.
3. [ ] Start a new session and ask for the list again. Notion's tools should be gone while Context7's should remain.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

lessons.title: Computer Use
lessons.readme:
# Computer Use

Coding agents are happiest when they can use _precise_ tools. Reading a file is easier with a `read` tool than by opening an editor and dragging a mouse over the text. Sometimes, though, the graphical user interface (GUI) _is_ the thing that needs to be tested.

**Computer use** lets a model inspect a screen and operate graphical applications with actions like clicking, typing, scrolling, and switching windows. [ChatGPT Computer Use](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/computer-use) and [Claude's computer use](https://claude.com/resources/articles/dispatch-and-computer-use) build these controls directly into their desktop applications.

OpenCode doesn't currently include a general-purpose desktop controller. That said, it can still operate browsers through external tools, which is where most coding-related computer use happens anyway!

## Feedback Loop

Computer use gives an agent another way to gather runtime evidence:

1. Observe the current interface.
2. Perform an action.
3. Inspect what changed.
4. Repeat until the behavior is correct.

That's the same feedback loop used with tests, logs, and compiler errors, but now the evidence is "closer to the user" because it's the same graphical interface they interact with.

I recommend using a direct API, command, or structured tool for feedback **when one exists**. Having a model click through a UI is slower and less reliable, but sometimes it's the only reasonable option! If you're making changes to the UI of a website, it's great that the model can check that the [DOM](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document_Object_Model) looks good, but that's not much consolation if the rendered button is bleeding halfway outside its container.

> [!danger]
>
> Computer-use tools can read visible data, use active browser sessions, click destructive controls, and submit forms. It's like giving another person access to your mouse and keyboard, so be very careful about what permissions you allow – particularly to an all-encompassing multimodal agent like Claude Cowork or ChatGPT Desktop.

lessons.title: Browser Automation
lessons.readme:
# Browser Automation

Now, a browser is still a graphical application, but it does expose way more structure than your typical native desktop app. It makes sense: web apps are built on structured text! So text-based browser automation tools can easily inspect:

- The document structure
- The accessibility tree
- Console messages
- Network requests
- Page layout measurements

That means a text-first agent like OpenCode can still fill the `Company` field by name, click the `Add application` button, and then check that the new row appeared. It doesn't even need an image model to guess where the button's pixels happen to be.

## Browser Feedback Loops

OpenCode can drive a browser automatically to run a full validation loop, like this:

1. Start the application.
2. Open the page in a (usually [headless](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/automation-and-testing/headless)) browser.
3. Reproduce the bug with the same clicks a user would make.
4. Inspect the DOM, developer console, and network activity.
5. Fix the code and run the flow again.

This works _incredibly well_ for exploration and debugging – and you'll get much better results than if you just had the model one-shot a solution before you checked it manually. That said, you **still do need to check** it manually.

Vision-enabled models that can actually use the computer will catch _more_ visual bugs than a text-only model, but they won't catch everything, and they still lack _taste_.

lessons.title: Accessibility Trees
lessons.readme:
# Accessibility Trees

A screenshot can tell a model what a page _looks like_, but an [accessibility tree](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Accessibility_tree) tells it what all the controls _mean_.

Luckily, browsers build the accessibility tree straight from the DOM. It contains semantic information that assistive technology and browser tools can understand:

- **Name:** `Add application`
- **Role:** `button`
- **State:** `enabled`
- **Description:** Extra context when the name isn't enough

A simplified snapshot looks kinda like this:

```text
- heading "Applications" [level=1]
- button "Add application"
- textbox "Company"
- combobox "Status" [value="Applied"]
```

Because the accessibility tree (when snapshotted) is just concise plain text, an agent can target those controls by _meaning_ instead of trying to estimate screen coordinates. So for most use cases, it's faster, more reliable, and works with a text-only model.

## What the Tree Misses

The accessibility tree doesn't describe every pixel. It won't reliably tell the agent that:

- Two buttons overlap
- Text is clipped
- A mobile layout overflows the screen
- A chart drawn on a canvas looks wrong

Also, bad HTML can produce a bad accessibility tree. If your front-end code sucks – like using `div`s for everything instead of [semantic HTML5](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Core/Accessibility/HTML) – the accessibility tree will miss a lot of important information.

If you write clean semantic HTML (and instruct your agent to do so as well), agents will have a much better time working on your project.

lessons.title: Vision Models
lessons.readme:
# Vision Models

A **vision model** can accept image input along with text. Instead of reading a semantic description of a page, it can inspect the screenshot's pixels.

OpenCode [supports image attachments](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/attachments) and passes image results from tools to models that can accept them. Not every model does, so be sure to check a model's capabilities before you pay for a bunch of tokens or a subscription.

Pixels sometimes expose problems that structured browser data simply can't:

- Awkward spacing
- Clipped or overlapping content
- Broken responsive layouts
- Charts, canvases, and other graphical output
- A page that technically works but looks like a Craigslist ad from 2004

> [!theo]
>
> I actually find it refreshing when a page looks like 20-year-old basic HTML, but that's beside the point...

## Pixels Are Bad Selectors

Images are great for judging the rendered result, but they're a ~~bad~~ slow and clunky way for an agent to actually interact with the page.

A vision model can estimate where a button sits and click those coordinates. That _usually_ works, but the coordinates are brittle, and frankly, computer use is pretty slow compared to interacting with structured browser data. Let your agent use browser data to find and operate normal controls, _then_ have it use image input to judge the rendered result.

The accessibility tree handles the clicks, and the vision model answers, "Does this page look right?" To be fair, most agents' idea of "right" is probably different from yours, but it should at least be able to notice and fix _obvious_ visual problems.

## Assignment

3. [ ] Drag and drop the screenshot file into OpenCode, or give the agent the path to the screenshot.
4. [ ] Tell OpenCode to fix the layout in `playground/index.html`, keeping output readable at both narrow and desktop widths.
5. [ ] Reload the page and compare the result at both widths.

lessons.readme:
# Playwright MCP

[Playwright MCP](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp) gives an agent control of a real browser via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It can navigate pages, inspect accessibility snapshots, fill forms, click controls, and capture screenshots. To enable this MCP server, add the following to `opencode.jsonc`:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "playwright": {
        "type": "local",
        "command": [
          "bunx",
          "--bun",
          "@playwright/mcp@0.0.80",
          "--isolated",
          "--browser",
          "chromium",
        ],
      },
    },
  },
}
```

The `--isolated` flag starts the browser with a temporary profile. Cookies and local storage disappear when the session closes, which is exactly what we want for repeatable local testing. The `--browser chromium` option selects Chromium.

## Structured Control

Playwright MCP uses accessibility snapshots by default. A text-only model can locate a button by its role and name, click it, then inspect the updated page. Coordinate-based vision tools are optional, and you'll be able to use them only if you're working with an image-capable model:

```json
"command": ["bunx", "--bun", "@playwright/mcp@0.0.80", "--isolated", "--browser", "chromium", "--caps=vision"]
```

## Assignment

**Have OpenCode run a program through the playground's browser interface.** This code:

```slop

```

prints `browser slop 42` on one line.

1. [ ] Tell OpenCode to configure the `playwright` server shown above using Bun.
2. [ ] Have it add `.playwright-mcp/` to `.gitignore` so Playwright MCP's local browser data stays out of the repository.
3. [ ] Have OpenCode start the playground if needed, then use Playwright MCP to open it, enter the code above, and click **Run**.
4. [ ] Inspect the browser tool results and confirm the page displays `browser slop 42`. Have OpenCode read the new entry in `logs/runs.log` as well and confirm that it worked as expected.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

lessons.readme:
# Chrome DevTools MCP

[Chrome DevTools MCP](https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp) can navigate, click, fill forms, inspect semantic page snapshots, and take screenshots. That overlaps with Playwright MCP, to be fair, but Chrome DevTools goes deeper into Chrome itself.

This tool can also inspect:

- Console messages and source-mapped errors
- Network requests and responses
- [Lighthouse audits](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/overview)
- Performance traces
- JavaScript memory usage (with the `--memory-debugging` flag)

To enable this MCP server in `opencode.jsonc`:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "mcp": {
    "servers": {
      "chrome-devtools": {
        "type": "local",
        "command": [
          "bunx",
          "--bun",
          "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest",
          "--isolated",
        ],
      },
    },
  },
}
```

> [!info]
>
> You'll need [Bun](https://bun.com/docs/installation) and [Google Chrome](https://www.google.com/chrome/) installed for this to work.

## Which to Use

I often use the **Playwright MCP** for user flows and cross-browser automation, and **Chrome DevTools MCP** to let my agent dig deeper into browser internals like network requests, console messages, and performance traces.

Chrome DevTools also has optional coordinate-based tools behind the `--experimental-vision` flag, but the same rule applies: prefer semantic targets when the browser provides them.

## Assignment


3. [ ] Tell it to fix the page so it displays both the earlier output and the runtime error. Repeat the browser flow and inspect the rendered result, making sure the bug is actually fixed.

# Install Plugins

If you want to install someone else's plugin, just add the relevant [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/) package name to the [`plugins`](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/plugins#configure) array in `opencode.jsonc`:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "plugins": ["opencode-example-plugin", "@my-org/custom-plugin"],
}
```

OpenCode installs each package and its dependencies in a separate cache directory.

Again, list the plugin in project config if it's meant to be shared with collaborators, or in your global config for personal setup.

## List Plugins

The CLI can list the currently configured plugins, showing the ID, version, and source of each:

```sh
opencode plugin list
```

By default, OpenCode's built-in plugins are excluded. To include those as well:

```sh
opencode plugin list --builtin
```

# Plugin Hooks

[Hooks](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins#hooks) let plugins intercept live OpenCode operations and inspect or modify them.

OpenCode provides a variety of runtime hooks. Here are some examples (_not_ exhaustive):

- `ctx.tool.hook("execute.before", callback)` runs before a tool executes
- `ctx.tool.hook("execute.after", callback)` runs after a tool succeeds or fails
- `ctx.session.hook("context", callback)` modifies the system prompt, messages, or tools before a model call
- `ctx.session.hook("http.request", callback)` inspects or modifies a provider request
- `ctx.session.hook("http.response", callback)` inspects or replaces a provider response

**Transforms** change the _definitions_ of tools, skills, agents, etc. **Hooks** intercept live _operations_.

Hook callbacks run in the order they're registered. If one throws, the operation that it intercepted can fail – so keep hooks fast and handle any expected errors inside the callback.

## Assignment

**Log successful file changes** with a plugin hook. Use this SlopLang program to try it:

```slop
clanker describe(enabled) {
    vibe enabled {
        ship “hooks” + “ work”✨
    }
    ship “hooks failed”✨
}
hallucinate(describe(✅))✨
```

This calls `describe` with `✅` (true), so it joins two strings and returns `hooks work`, which `hallucinate` prints.

1. [ ] Tell OpenCode to create `.opencode/plugins/edit-log.ts`. After each successful `edit`, `write`, or `patch` call, the plugin should append a JSON line to `logs/plugin-tools.log` containing the `tool` name and a `status` of `completed`.
2. [ ] `/reload` OpenCode, then tell it to add `examples/hooks.slop` with the code above. Inspect the file-changing tool call and its matching log entry, then have it run the example to confirm the output.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

# Publishing Plugins

An OpenCode plugin published on npm uses the same default export as a local plugin. So if you want to publish a plugin, you can treat it as a normal ECMAScript module (ESM), with the plugin runtime listed in `dependencies`:

```json
{
  "name": "my-slop-opencode-plugin",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": "./dist/index.js",
  "dependencies": {
    "@opencode/plugin": "2.0.3"
  }
}
```

The `exports` field identifies the file OpenCode loads. There are two options:

- **Compiled JavaScript:** Use `"exports": "./dist/index.js"` as above, compile the plugin's TypeScript code, and include the generated files in the published package.
- **TypeScript source:** Use `"exports": "./src/index.ts"` and include the source files in the published package. OpenCode [can load TypeScript directly](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins#publish).

answers: The location of the published plugin

lessons.readme:
# Accountability

As an AI-enabled software engineer, now more than ever (although this has _always been true_), the value you provide to your team is **not** the number of lines of code you ~~generate~~ write.

Also, no matter how great an agent is at producing code, the CEO of a company isn't going to spend all their time prompting the agent to code for them. **They have other things to do** (at least, the good ones...).

![responsibility](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/responsibility-1920x1080.mp4)

You _do_ offer value in your:

- Ability to understand the code the agent produces – not just _what_ it does, but _why_ that's **a good way** to do it.
- Expertise to protect the codebase from vulnerabilities.
- Judgment to know when to push back on a feature because it will add too much complexity/latency/cost for the value it provides.
- Time and care that you put into prompting, re-prompting, and fixing AI-generated code, and ensuring its safe rollout.

Perhaps most importantly, you provide **your own end-to-end accountability** for the code you ship.

## It's Not How the Sausage Is Made

It really doesn't matter to your users _or your team_ how each individual line of code in your PRs was written.

- Did you type it at 150 wpm in Neovim?
- Did you copy/paste it from Stack Overflow?
- Did your agent generate it for you?

_No one cares_.

The bottom line is that the code is _your responsibility_, and saying "The agent wrote it" is _not_ an excuse for bad code. In fact, it's a _worse_ excuse than "I wrote it" because if you wrote it, at least you were trying. **I'd rather have a team member who tries and fails than one who wants to be lazy and redirect blame.**

questions.question: Who is responsible for the code you ship if an agent wrote it?
questions.answer: You

questions.question: Where does the best code always come from?
questions.answer: The source doesn't matter.

lessons.title: Evidence Debugging
lessons.readme:
# Evidence Debugging

Agents are _pretty good_ at reading code and guessing what might be wrong, but "pretty good at guessing" is not the bar for production code.

The most effective tactic for AI debugging is to push it toward **concrete evidence** as quickly as possible:

- Traces
- Structured logs
- Failing test outputs
- Reproduction scripts
- User reports/issues
- Real request/response payloads with secrets removed

## Don't Let It Patch Blindly

For debugging tasks, use prompts that explicitly _forbid_ speculative fixes:

> Before changing behavior, generate hypotheses, add temporary structured instrumentation, reproduce the bug, and explain which evidence confirms the root cause.

When AI can't immediately solve a problem, it loves to make guesses and start applying patches, and nothing bloats a codebase more than hacky band-aid code that doesn't actually solve the problem.

## Assignment

**Reproduce and fix a variable-assignment bug.** This code:

```slop
slop score = 1✨
{
    slop score = 2✨
    {
        score = 3✨
    }
    hallucinate(score)✨
}
hallucinate(score)✨
```

creates two separate variables named `score`. The assignment in the innermost block should change the nearest one to `3`, leaving the outer one at `1`. It should print `3` and `1` on separate lines, but currently prints `2` and `3`!

1. [ ] Tell OpenCode to save the code above in `examples/scope-repro.slop` and run it before changing the interpreter. Inspect the incorrect output.
2. [ ] Have it trace the incorrect assignment using that output, fix the cause, and add a regression test in a new file named `tests/test_scope_assignment.py`.

Tell OpenCode to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the project root.

lessons.readme:
# Refactoring

[Refactoring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_refactoring) is when you take some code that does something, and change it!

... to do the exact same thing.

Well, the same thing **in a better way**. By "better," we usually mean:

- More readable
- More maintainable
- More extensible

The behavior of the code doesn't change, but the structure does. Sometimes you can remove hundreds of lines of code (yay!). Sometimes you add a few lines, but now it's so much easier to understand (also yay!).

My favorite refactors are when you update the architectural structure of the code (oftentimes by moving around the abstraction layers), and now a feature that was going to touch 500 lines of code now only changes 40. **This is common, but it requires developer expertise.**

## Be Purposeful About Refactoring

Almost all changes to a codebase are one of three types:

1. New features
2. Bug fixes
3. Refactors

New developers often underestimate the importance of _dedicated refactor commits_. Do them!

## AI Is Good at Refactoring

Refactoring is _more_ important with AI, not less. Because AI agents can sling so much garbage text so fast, you don't need to optimize for the number of lines written (sorry [Garry](https://bcantrill.dtrace.org/2026/04/12/the-peril-of-laziness-lost/)). Try to maximize the percentage of AI-produced lines of code **that you don't have to manually fix**.

AI is really good at refactoring. It has all the file-editing tools. You can give it style guides. It has context; it has examples.

The problem is that _it won't do it_, or at least _it won't do it well_, if you don't tell it how. Make that part of your workflow.

## Assignment

**Refactor the arithmetic code without changing its behavior.** For example, this code:

```slop
hallucinate(7 + 2, 7 - 2, 7 * 2, -7 / 2)✨
```

should still print `9 5 14 -3`. Division should truncate toward zero.

2. [ ] Review the diff and have it run the full validation suite.

lessons.readme:
# Good Code

Perhaps counterintuitively, in a world with AI coding agents, _great codebases_ are more important than before. You'll hear business people opining that "the code doesn't matter anymore" or "the cost of producing software is going to zero," but those are **uninformed opinions** from non-technical people. Sorry not sorry.

Agents **primarily** want to finish the task in front of them. They do **not** inherently care about:

- The engineer who will read this code two months from now
- The next task in your Jira backlog that will build on this change
- The function on line 117 that seems to do nothing, but which Steve said NOT TO TOUCH because prod breaks in weird ways if you delete it

It's **your** job to care about that stuff. You have much more than a single ephemeral window of context about your codebase, team, company, and users.

## Two Truths

1. AI agents can make you _more_ productive in a great codebase.
2. AI agents can turn a good codebase into a bad one _rapidly_.

## Aiming the Slop Cannon

When you prompt, be sure to demand things that you care about:

- Minimal diffs
- Existing patterns over novelty
- Clear naming conventions

But just asking the clanker _is still not enough_. You always have to review the code, understand the architecture of the project, and yes, **very often** you will still need to force the agent to go down a different path from what it initially thought was best.

# Incremental Changes

I'm not gonna lie, it does feel _really_ nice when you write a fat, detailed prompt and refine it with the agent, then the agent one-shots a 1,000-line change in almost exactly the way you wanted it.

And that _does_ happen.

But you can also waste a lot of time pulling the slot machine lever again and again, hoping for that sweet jackpot.

When you _can_ break a change into smaller steps, it's still a good idea to do so. Context isn't infinite, and the smaller the changeset, the quicker it is to get the agent back on track when it inevitably isn't doing quite what you want.

## Assignment

**Add support for `+=` in two small changes.** This code:

```slop
slop n = 2✨
n += 3 * 4✨
hallucinate(n)✨
```

should print `14`. The `+=` operator adds to the variable's current value, but the right-hand expression is evaluated first, so `3 * 4` adds `12` to `n`.

It should also join strings and update the nearest variable with that name. Undefined names, immutable variables, and incompatible types should produce runtime errors.

1. [ ] Tell OpenCode to make Sloperator recognize and parse `+=`, and to add new tests in `tests/test_compound_assignment_parser.py`. Stop before making the new operator execute assignments. Inspect the diff and have it run those tests.
2. [ ] Next, tell it to make `+=` execute with the behavior above, update `docs/spec.md`, and add regression tests in `tests/test_compound_assignment.py`.

lessons.title: Workflow
lessons.readme:
# Workflow

The tasks you work on will vary from single-line changes to multi-file features that require new infrastructure to be deployed.

That means sometimes your workflow will be as simple as one-shotting a single-sentence prompt. Other times, it will be a full 30-message back and forth with the agent before you even let it change a single line. And sometimes, you'll still execute the change (gasp) _by hand_.

That said, in most cases, the following basic workflow will serve you well. Have the agent:

1. **Explore** the codebase and constraints
2. **Plan** the change if it's non-trivial
3. **Implement** the smallest correct version
4. **Verify** with real feedback loops

## Why This Works

Planning and implementing are obvious steps – and hopefully, verifying is too. The most overlooked part in my experience is the first step: **exploring** the codebase, the constraints, documentation, and more.

Without _really good context_, the agent's plan is going to be suboptimal. The "way to build a notes feature" is going to look very different for a local-first app like Obsidian than it will for a realtime web-based app like Google Docs. Don't be afraid to force the agent to go read!

And exploring shouldn't be limited to the codebase. Agents have the `webfetch` tool! Make it do research about common approaches, which libraries exist, and anything else you think might be relevant.
