lessons.readme:
# Multiple Agents

Are you _ready for the hack_? The one trick that can **finally make you a 10x engineer**?

... okay, maybe not. But a 1.2x engineer? Or a 2x engineer? In my experience, it's closer to 1.5x.

The trick is **multiple agents**.

If all you do is prompt your agent, and then just sit there with a blank stare on your face ~~while you contemplate the meaninglessness of this existence and whether you'll ever find true love~~, you probably won't be much more productive than if you were to just type the change yourself. Agents can produce code quickly, but part of the reason their slop is _remotely tolerable_ is because they go through **so many** tool calls and iterations before showing you the result.

And that's _slow_.

So, oftentimes the real productivity boost comes from the fact that you can go do something else while you wait. Unfortunately, if you just spin up another instance of OpenCode in the same directory, the two agents can step on each other's work.

## Use Git Worktrees

While you _can_ simply copy your entire codebase into another directory and have a second agent work there, that's pretty clunky. Frankly, I almost never used the [`git worktree`](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree) command before I started coding with AI, but now I use it **all the time**.

A Git worktree is a way to switch to another [`git branch`](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-branch), but actually work on that branch in another directory on the same machine. The worktree is still linked to the original Git repository, so you can easily share and merge the changes when you're done.

We cover worktrees in our [Git 2](https://www.boot.dev/courses/learn-git-2) course. I won't rehash it all here, but the basic commands are:

```sh
# create a new worktree at FILEPATH
git worktree add FILEPATH

# list all worktrees
git worktree list
```

The key benefit of a worktree is that it provides a separate working directory while sharing the same Git repository and history. Each agent can work on its own branch without touching another agent's in-progress files.

I usually have two worktrees per project, one agent running in each. Honestly, I've tried to run three agents at a time, but the context-switching (at least for me) gets to be too much at that point. I'd only go that far if an agent were going to churn for literal _hours_ unsupervised.

## Assignment

**Run two reviews in separate working directories** so the agents don't interfere with each other's files.

1. [ ] Use `/commit Finish Sloperator` to commit your project, then tell OpenCode to create a sibling worktree at `../sloperator-dev` on a new `dev` branch.
2. [ ] Open a second OpenCode session in that worktree. Have it install the project dependencies and review the evaluator while the original session reviews the parser. Ask both agents to report their working directory before starting.
3. [ ] Compare their findings and confirm each session stayed in its assigned directory.

Tell the original OpenCode session to **run and submit** the CLI tests from the original project root.

lessons.readme:
# Keep Learning

Compared to current agents, agents from six months ago are _mouthbreathers_. Until proven otherwise, we can expect that pace of change to continue.

This course contains the current best practices, but we can expect the SOTA to change. This course is updated constantly to stay evergreen, but realize _you_ need to stay up to date, too.

## Models Are Increasingly Capable

Each new SOTA model release seemingly aims to correct the previous model's flaws based on users' feedback. It's not that they are necessarily _smarter_, they are just _trained_ on more relevant data and tasks. What that means for you is your AGENTS.md, skills, and tools might already be **obsolete**.

The newest models:

- Don't make the same mistakes
- Know how to do more things
- Need less babysitting

Review your setup for each new model to see what you simply don't need anymore. Over time, you should _remove more prompting_ than you add.

## Agent Harnesses Are Constantly Improving

OpenCode and (most) other coding agents are constantly updated to adapt to the latest models and use cases. What you use a plugin or tool for now could become a feature later. A feature you rely on currently might be eliminated down the road.

Embrace the change to your workflow. You should customize your preferred coding agent _as little as possible_ for best results.
